fields.title: The Gospel of Luke
fields.subtitle: Kata Loukan, “According to Luke”
fields.description: The longest of the four Gospels, written by a careful historian “in order” so that his reader could be sure of what he had been taught: “The Son of Man came to look for what was lost and to save it.” Gabriel’s visits to Zechariah and Mary; the songs of Mary, Zechariah, the angels and Simeon; the shepherds and the manger; Jesus’s first sermon at Nazareth, good news to the poor; the long journey to Jerusalem with the good Samaritan, the lost sheep, the lost coin and the lost son, the rich man and Lazarus, and Zacchaeus up his tree. Then the prayer “Father, forgive them”, the promise of paradise to a dying criminal, and the risen Jesus made known on the road to Emmaus in the breaking of the bread. The first of Luke’s two volumes, continued in Acts. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Gospel of Luke?
qa.answer: The third of the four Gospels, the accounts of the life, death and resurrection of Jesus in the New Testament, and the first of a two-part work completed by the Acts of the Apostles. It tells more of Jesus’s birth than any other Gospel, and many of his best-loved parables are found only here, among them the good Samaritan and the lost son. It shows Jesus bringing good news to the poor, the sinful and the outsider: in his own words, “The Son of Man came to look for what was lost and to save it” (19:10).

qa.question: Who wrote the Gospel of Luke, and when?
qa.answer: The Gospel does not name its author, but it and Acts are addressed to the same Theophilus and written by the same hand. From the second century the church has said the author was Luke, the doctor and companion of Paul (Colossians 4:14), and the passages in Acts told in the first person (“we”) suggest he travelled with Paul. He says he was not an eyewitness but drew on those who were (1:1–4). Suggested dates range from the early 60s to the 80s.

qa.question: What is the parable of the prodigal son about?
qa.answer: It is the third of three stories in Luke 15 that Jesus tells when religious leaders complain that he welcomes sinners and eats with them: a lost sheep, a lost coin and a lost son. A younger son wastes his inheritance and comes home, and his father runs to meet him and throws a feast. Each story ends in rejoicing over what was lost and is found. The elder brother, who refuses to come in, is left outside with his father pleading with him, and the parable ends without saying whether he went in.

qa.question: Why is Luke called the Gospel of prayer and of the Holy Spirit?
qa.answer: Luke shows Jesus praying more often than any other Gospel: at his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, at the transfiguration, for Peter, in Gethsemane and on the cross; and only Luke tells the parables of the friend at midnight and the persistent widow. He also tells of the Spirit filling Elizabeth, Zechariah and Simeon, coming upon Mary and resting on Jesus, and records Jesus’s promise that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask (11:13), a promise fulfilled in Acts.

qa.question: Where does Luke 2:7 say Jesus was born?
qa.answer: Older Bibles say there was “no room at the inn”. The Greek word is the one Luke uses for the upper room of the last supper, a guest room in a house, not his word for an inn; so this translation says “the guest room had no space for them”. Joseph and Mary were probably staying in a house whose guest room was full, and the baby was laid in a feeding trough, a manger, where the animals were fed.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
The Son of Man came to look for what was lost and to save it.”

— Luke 19:10

Luke is the only Gospel writer who tells us, in his own voice, how he went about his work. He begins with a single long sentence, in the polished style of a Greek historian, addressed to a man named Theophilus:

Many people have set their hands to putting together an account of the events that have been brought to completion among us. They wrote them down as they were passed on to us by those who saw them from the beginning and became servants of the word. So I too, having followed the whole course of things closely from the start, decided to write them out for you in order, most excellent Theophilus, so that you can be sure of the things you were taught.

— Luke 1:1–4

He was not an eyewitness himself, he says. Others had already written accounts. He had gone back over the whole course of things from the start, drawing on what had been handed down by those who saw it, and set it out in order, so that his reader could be sure. It is a modest and serious beginning, and it tells us what kind of book this is: a careful account, by a man who cared about getting things right, of the events that changed the world.

And then, a few verses later, the polished Greek gives way to the language of the Old Testament, and we are in the temple at Jerusalem, where an old priest is burning incense and an angel is standing beside the altar. Luke can write like a historian. But the story he has to tell is full of angels and songs, of the poor lifted up and the lost found, and of a joy that keeps breaking out.

The beloved physician

The Gospel does not name its author, but its second volume, the Acts of the Apostles, is addressed to the same Theophilus and begins by recalling “the first book”. From the second century the church has said that both were written by Luke, a companion of Paul. Paul mentions him three times: as “Our dear friend Luke, the doctor”, as a fellow worker, and, near the end of his life, in a single plain sentence, “Only Luke is with me.” In Colossians Paul seems to list him apart from his Jewish fellow workers, and many readers think Luke was a Gentile, the only non-Jewish author in the New Testament.

Several passages in Acts slip from “they” into “we”, as if the writer was there, travelling with Paul. Most readers have taken them that way; some scholars think they come from a travel diary the author used, or are a literary device. Irenaeus, around 180, calls Luke “the companion of Paul” and says he recorded in a book the gospel Paul preached. Together, Luke and Acts make up more than a quarter of the New Testament, more than any other single writer.

Dates suggested for the Gospel range from the early 60s to the 80s. Like Matthew, Luke seems to have used Mark, and a collection of Jesus’s sayings that the two share; but a great deal of his Gospel, perhaps a third or more, is found nowhere else.

Luke is also the Gospel writer who most often ties his story to the wider world. Jesus is born when “an order went out from Caesar Augustus” for a registration of the empire, “while Quirinius was governor of Syria”. John the Baptist’s work begins in “the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar”, which is about AD 28, and Luke names the governor, the local rulers and the high priests of that year. Historians have long debated how the census fits what is known of Quirinius, and the question is not settled. But Luke’s point is plain. Nothing in this story happened out of sight. It happened in the real world of emperors and taxes, to people with names.

A Gospel that sings

The first two chapters of Luke are among the most loved in the Bible, and almost all of their contents are his alone: the angel Gabriel’s visit to Zechariah, and then to Mary at Nazareth; Mary’s visit to her cousin Elizabeth; the birth of John; the census, the journey to Bethlehem, the shepherds and the angels; the old man Simeon and the prophet Anna in the temple; and the boy Jesus, twelve years old, sitting among the teachers.

These chapters are full of songs, and the church has sung them ever since. Mary’s song, the Magnificat, begins:

And Mary said, “My soul declares the greatness of the Lord, and my spirit has found its delight in God my Savior,

— Luke 1:46–47

Zechariah sings when his tongue is loosed; the angels praise God, “Glory to God in the heights of heaven”; and Simeon, holding the child in his arms, sings that he can now die in peace, because his eyes have seen the salvation God has prepared, “a light of revelation for the nations, and the glory of your people Israel.” In these songs the whole Old Testament seems to rise up to greet the child. They are full of Abraham and David, of promises remembered and mercy shown. And they announce, before Jesus has said a word, what kind of king he will be. In Mary’s words, God “has pulled the mighty down from their thrones and raised up the lowly.”

Luke’s story begins and ends in the temple: with Zechariah praying there in the first chapter, and with the disciples there in the last, “blessing God”.

Good news to the poor

Luke sets the first scene of Jesus’s public work in the synagogue of his home town. He is handed the scroll of Isaiah, finds the place, and reads:

“The Spirit of the Lord rests on me, for he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. He has sent me to announce freedom to the captives and sight to the blind, to set the downtrodden free, and to announce the year when the Lord shows favor.”

— Luke 4:18–19

Then he rolls up the scroll, sits down, and with every eye fixed on him says, “Today, as you have been listening, these words of Scripture have come true.” The rest of the Gospel unfolds that reading. Again and again Luke shows Jesus with people whom others pass by: the poor, the sick, the sinful, the grieving, the foreigner. In Luke’s beatitudes it is simply “you poor” who are blessed, and he adds woes for the rich. The first to hear of the Saviour’s birth are shepherds in the fields. Jesus raises a widow’s only son at Nain because “pity for her moved him deeply”. He lets a woman known in the town as a sinner wash his feet with her tears, and tells her that her sins stand forgiven. Of ten lepers healed, the only one who comes back to give thanks is a Samaritan. And on the road through Jericho, Jesus invites himself to the house of Zacchaeus, the chief tax collector, and says: “Today salvation has come to this household.”

Luke also has more to say about women than any other Gospel writer. Elizabeth, Mary and Anna open the story. Women travel with Jesus and the Twelve, “using their own resources to provide for them”, among them Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna. Martha’s sister Mary sits at the Lord’s feet as a disciple would. And it is women who are the first to hear that he is risen.

Money, too, is never far from Luke’s mind. Jesus warns that life “does not come from the things a person owns”, and tells of a rich farmer who built bigger barns and died that night, of a rich man who feasted every day while a beggar named Lazarus lay at his gate, and of a dishonest manager who used money to make friends. Zacchaeus gives half of what he owns to the poor; the rich ruler goes away filled with sorrow.

The journey to Jerusalem

Midway through the Gospel there is a turning:

As the time drew near for him to be taken up, he turned his face toward Jerusalem, determined to go there. He sent messengers on ahead of him.

— Luke 9:51–52

From here until Jesus enters Jerusalem in chapter 19, nearly ten chapters, Luke presents his story as one long journey. It is not a travel itinerary, and the places are rarely named. It is the road to the cross, and along it Luke has gathered much of the teaching that only he records. Here are the parables that have entered the language of the world: the good Samaritan; the friend at midnight; the rich fool; the lost sheep, the lost coin and the lost son; the rich man and Lazarus; the persistent widow; the Pharisee and the tax collector.

Lost and found

The heart of the journey, and for many readers the heart of the whole Bible, is chapter 15. It begins with a complaint. Tax collectors and sinners are gathering to listen to Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes complain. “This man welcomes sinners,” they say, “and even shares meals with them.” Jesus answers with three stories: a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to search for one, a woman who sweeps the house for a lost coin, and a father with two sons.

The younger son takes his inheritance, wastes it in a far country, and comes home rehearsing a speech. He never finishes it:

His father caught sight of him while he was still far away, and his heart went out to him. He ran to meet him, embraced him and kissed him warmly.

— Luke 15:20

Each of the three stories ends in a party, because something lost has been found, and each says the same thing: there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. But the third story has a second son, the elder brother, who has never left home and will not come in to the feast. Jesus leaves him standing outside, with his father pleading with him. It is an open ending, addressed to the people who were muttering at the start of the chapter, and perhaps to us.

Prayer, the Spirit, and joy

Luke is the Gospel of prayer. Jesus is praying when the Spirit comes down on him at his baptism. He slips away to the wilderness to pray; he spends a whole night in prayer before choosing the Twelve; he is praying when he is transfigured; and it is after watching him pray that his disciples ask, “Lord, teach us how to pray.” Only Luke tells the parables of the friend who knocks at midnight and the widow who will not give up, both about praying without losing heart. And only Luke tells us that Jesus prayed for Peter, that his faith would not give out.

It is also the Gospel of the Holy Spirit. John the Baptist is filled with the Spirit before he is born; the Spirit comes upon Mary; Elizabeth, Zechariah and Simeon all speak by the Spirit. Jesus goes into the wilderness full of the Spirit and returns in the Spirit’s power, and he promises that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him. Luke’s second volume begins with that promise kept.

And it is the Gospel of joy. The angel brings “a great joy that is for all the people”; there is joy in heaven over the lost; the seventy-two return with joy; Jesus himself rejoices in the Holy Spirit; and the Gospel ends with the disciples going back to Jerusalem “with great joy”. One small word keeps sounding through it: today. Today a Saviour has been born; today this Scripture is fulfilled; today salvation has come to this house; today you will be with me in paradise.

The cross and the road to Emmaus

Luke’s account of the passion is his own in many details. Only Luke tells us that Jesus was sent to Herod, who mocked him; that an angel strengthened him in Gethsemane; that he healed the ear of the high priest’s servant; and that on the way to the cross he spoke to the women of Jerusalem who were weeping for him. Three of the sayings from the cross are found only here: the prayer for those who crucified him, “Father, forgive them. They do not know what they are doing”; the promise to the criminal beside him, “this very day you will be with me in paradise”; and his last words, a prayer from Psalm 31, “Father, I place my spirit in your hands.”

The resurrection chapter holds the loveliest story Luke tells. Two disciples are walking home to Emmaus on the first Easter Day, sad and confused, when a stranger falls into step with them and asks what they are discussing. As they walk, he goes through the Scriptures with them, “starting with Moses and going on through all the prophets”. At the village they press him to stay, and at the table he takes the bread, says the blessing, breaks it, and hands it to them:

Then their eyes were opened and they knew who he was. And he could no longer be seen.

— Luke 24:31

Then he appears to the eleven, eats a piece of fish in front of them to show he is no ghost, opens their minds to understand the Scriptures, and tells them to wait in the city until they are clothed with power from on high. And he leads them out as far as Bethany, blesses them, and is carried up into heaven.

How to read Luke

Notice its shape. The prologue (1:1–4) leads into the birth and childhood of John and Jesus (1:5–2:52); then the preparation for Jesus’s work (3:1–4:13), and the work in Galilee (4:14–9:50); the long journey to Jerusalem (9:51–19:27); and the last days in Jerusalem, the cross and the resurrection (19:28–24:53).

Read it with Acts beside it. Luke wrote the two as one work, and they echo each other everywhere: the Spirit coming on Jesus and then on the church, Jesus’s prayer for his killers and Stephen’s, a Gospel that ends in Jerusalem and a second volume that begins there and goes out to Rome.

And read it, as Luke would want, with your eyes on the people Jesus meets. Ask who is welcomed and who is offended, who is found and who stays outside. Luke wrote so that Theophilus could “be sure of the things you were taught”. He also wrote so that every reader could find himself or herself somewhere on the road, and be found.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Luke are worth knowing about before you begin.

The guest room and the feeding trough. In 2:7 the familiar “no room at the inn” reads “the guest room had no space for them”. Luke uses the same word for the upper room of the last supper, and a different word for an inn; Joseph and Mary were probably staying in a house whose guest room was full. The baby is laid in “a feeding trough”, which is what a manger is.

“Put right with God.” At the end of the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector (18:14), where older Bibles say the tax collector went home “justified”, this translation says what the word means: he “went home put right with God”.

Places where manuscripts differ. In 10:1 and 10:17 Jesus sends out seventy-two, where many manuscripts read seventy; the early copies are divided. The angel who strengthens Jesus in Gethsemane and his sweat like drops of blood (22:43–44), and the prayer “Father, forgive them” (23:34), are missing from some important early manuscripts but found in others; this translation includes them. Luke 17:36 and 23:17, which older Bibles print, are not in the earliest manuscripts and were probably added from Matthew and Mark; they are not in the text, and the verse numbers are skipped.

“Christ.” The Open Word Bible lets a reader choose whether Christos reads “Christ” or “the Messiah”. This edition prints “Christ”, as in the angel’s words to the shepherds, “a Savior has been born for you: Christ, the Lord.”

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Luke 1
fields.body_html:
An orderly account for Theophilus

Many people have set their hands to putting together an account of the events that have been brought to completion among us. They wrote them down as they were passed on to us by those who saw them from the beginning and became servants of the word. So I too, having followed the whole course of things closely from the start, decided to write them out for you in order, most excellent Theophilus, so that you can be sure of the things you were taught.

Gabriel comes to Zechariah in the temple

In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, who belonged to the priestly division of Abijah. His wife was also descended from Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. Both of them were righteous in God’s eyes, and they lived by every commandment and requirement of the Lord with no fault to be found in them. But they had no children, because Elizabeth could not conceive, and both of them were getting on in years.

Once, when Zechariah’s division was on duty and he was serving as priest before God, he was chosen by lot, as the custom of the priesthood was, to go into the sanctuary of the Lord and burn incense. At the hour of the incense offering, the whole crowd of people was praying outside. Then an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing to the right of the altar of incense. When Zechariah saw him, he was shaken, and fear came over him. But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah. Your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will give you a son, and you are to name him John. He will be your joy and delight, and many people will be glad that he was born. For he will be great in the sight of the Lord. He must never drink wine or beer, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even before he is born. He will bring many of the people of Israel back to the Lord their God. He will go ahead of him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers back to their children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, and so make ready a people prepared for the Lord.” Zechariah said to the angel, “How can I be sure of this? I am an old man, and my wife is getting on in years.” The angel answered him, “I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. And now you will be silent, unable to speak, until the day these things take place, because you did not believe my words. They will come true at their proper time.”

Meanwhile the people were waiting for Zechariah and wondering why he was staying so long in the sanctuary. When he came out, he could not speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the sanctuary. He kept making signs to them, but he remained unable to speak. When his days of service were over, he went home.

After this his wife Elizabeth became pregnant, and for five months she stayed in seclusion. “The Lord has done this for me,” she said. “In these days he has looked on me with favor and taken away my disgrace among people.”

Gabriel comes to Mary in Nazareth

In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent by God to Nazareth, a town of Galilee, to a virgin who was engaged to Joseph, a man of the house of David. Her name was Mary. He came to her and said, “Greetings! God has shown you his favor. The Lord is with you.” His words disturbed her deeply, and she kept asking herself what such a greeting could mean. The angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary. You have found favor with God. You will become pregnant and have a son, and you are to give him the name Jesus. He will be great, and he will be called Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of David, his forefather, and he will be king over the house of Jacob for all ages. There will be no end to his kingdom.” Mary said to the angel, “How can this happen? I have never been with a man.” The angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will cover you with its shadow. So the child to be born will be holy, and will be called the Son of God. Your relative Elizabeth, too, has conceived a son in her old age. People called her barren, yet this is her sixth month. For with God, no promise will prove impossible.” Mary said, “I am the Lord’s servant. Let it happen to me as you have said.” Then the angel left her.

Elizabeth greets the mother of her Lord

In those days Mary set out and hurried to a town in the hill country of Judah. She went into Zechariah’s house and greeted Elizabeth. As Mary’s greeting reached Elizabeth, the child in her womb leaped, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit. She cried out in a loud voice, “Of all women, you are the most blessed, and blessed is the child you carry! Who am I, that the mother of my Lord should come to visit me? The moment your greeting reached my ears, the child in my womb leaped with delight. Blessed is the woman who believed that what the Lord said to her would be carried out!”

Mary praises the Mighty One

And Mary said, “My soul declares the greatness of the Lord, and my spirit has found its delight in God my Savior, because he has looked with care on his servant in her lowly state. From this day people of every generation will call me blessed, for the Mighty One has done great things for me. Holy is his name, and his mercy reaches from one generation to the next for those who fear him.

He has acted with the strength of his arm; he has scattered the proud, with all the schemes of their hearts. He has pulled the mighty down from their thrones and raised up the lowly. The hungry he has filled with good things, and the rich he has sent away with nothing. He has come to the aid of his servant Israel and has not forgotten to show mercy, as he said to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever.”

Mary remained with Elizabeth about three months before returning home.

John is born and named

Elizabeth’s time to give birth came, and she bore a son. Her neighbors and relatives heard how greatly the Lord had shown his mercy to her, and they celebrated with her.

When the child was eight days old, they came to circumcise him, and they wanted to give him his father’s name, Zechariah. But his mother answered, “No. His name is to be John.” “But no one in your family is called by that name,” they said to her. Then they motioned to his father, asking what name he wanted the child to have. He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” Everyone was astonished. In that instant Zechariah’s mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he began to speak, giving praise to God. Awe came over all their neighbors, and throughout the hill country of Judea people were talking about all these things. Everyone who heard about them took them to heart and asked, “What then will this child turn out to be?” For the Lord’s hand was clearly with him.

Zechariah blesses the God of Israel

Then his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke this prophecy: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, for he has come to help his people and set them free. He has raised up a mighty power to save us in the house of his servant David, as he promised long ago through the mouth of his holy prophets: salvation from our enemies and from the grip of all who hate us. So he has shown the mercy promised to our ancestors and remembered his holy covenant, the oath he swore to our father Abraham: to grant us that we, rescued from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High, for you will go ahead of the Lord to prepare his ways, to make known to his people the salvation that comes through the forgiveness of their sins. Because our God is full of tender mercy, the dawn from on high will visit us, to give light to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, and to direct our steps onto the road of peace.”

As the child grew, he became strong in spirit, and he lived in the desert places until the day he showed himself to Israel.

fields.title: Luke 2
fields.body_html:
The birth of Jesus in David’s town

In those days an order went out from Caesar Augustus that a register should be made of the whole empire. This was the first registration, and it took place while Quirinius was governor of Syria. Everyone set out to be registered, each in their own town.

So Joseph too went up from Nazareth in Galilee to Judea, to David’s town, Bethlehem, since he was from the house and clan of David. He went to be registered together with Mary, who was engaged to him and was expecting a child. While they were there, the days of her pregnancy came to an end, and she bore her firstborn son. She wrapped him snugly in cloths and laid him in a feeding trough, because the guest room had no space for them.

Good news for shepherds

In the same area there were shepherds out in the open country, taking turns to guard their flock through the night. An angel of the Lord stood before them, and the glory of the Lord blazed around them, and they were struck with great fear. But the angel said to them, “Do not fear. I am bringing you good news, a great joy that is for all the people. Today, in David’s town, a Savior has been born for you: Christ, the Lord. The sign for you is this: you will find a baby, wrapped snugly in cloths and lying in a feeding trough.” All at once the angel was joined by a great crowd of heaven’s army, who praised God and said, “Glory to God in the heights of heaven, and on earth peace to the people he favors!”

When the angels had gone back into heaven, the shepherds said to each other, “Come on, let us go across to Bethlehem and look at what has taken place, what the Lord has told us.” They made haste, and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in the feeding trough. When they saw the child, they told everyone what they had been told about him. All who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds told them. But Mary kept all these things close and turned them over in her heart. The shepherds went back, glorifying God and praising him for all they had heard and seen. It had been just as they were told.

Jesus is named and presented in the temple

Eight days later, when the time came for his circumcision, he was given the name Jesus, as the angel had called him before he was conceived.

When the time came for their purification under the law of Moses, they took him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord. For it is written in the law of the Lord, “Every firstborn male shall be called holy to the Lord.” They also came to offer the sacrifice that the law of the Lord requires: “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”

Simeon sees God’s salvation

Now in Jerusalem there lived a man called Simeon, upright and reverent, who longed for the day God would comfort Israel. The Holy Spirit was on him. The Holy Spirit had made known to him that he would not die until he had seen the Lord’s Christ. Guided by the Spirit, Simeon went into the temple. Jesus’s parents were bringing the child in, to carry out for him what the law’s custom required, and Simeon took him up in his arms, blessed God and said, “Master, now you are letting your servant go in peace, as you promised, because my eyes have seen the salvation that comes from you, which you have prepared in full view of every people: a light of revelation for the nations, and the glory of your people Israel.” His father and mother stood amazed at what was being said about him. Then Simeon blessed them and said to Mary, his mother, “This child is set to make many in Israel fall and rise again. He will be a sign that people oppose, and a sword will go through your own soul as well, so that the thoughts of many hearts will come to light.”

Anna speaks of the child

A prophet was there too, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was very old. She had married as a young woman and lived with her husband seven years, and she had been a widow ever since; she was now eighty-four. She never left the temple, but served God night and day with fasting and prayer. She came up just then, gave thanks to God, and went on speaking about him to everyone who was waiting for God to set Jerusalem free.

The child grows in Nazareth

When they had carried out everything the law of the Lord required, they went back to Galilee, to Nazareth, their own town.

The child kept growing and gaining strength. He was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God rested on him.

In his Father’s house

Year by year his parents used to go up to Jerusalem for the feast of Passover. When he was twelve, they went up as the custom of the feast was. After the days of the feast were over, as they set off for home, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem without his parents knowing. Thinking he was with the others on the road, they travelled for a whole day; then they began hunting for him among their relatives and the people they knew. Not finding him, they turned back to Jerusalem, still searching for him. Three days later they found him in the temple, seated among the teachers, listening to them and putting questions to them. Everyone who heard him was astounded at how much he understood and at the answers he gave. When his parents saw him, they were stunned, and his mother said to him, “My child, why have you treated us like this? Your father and I have been looking for you, sick with worry.” He said to them, “Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?” But they did not grasp what he meant. So he went back down with them to Nazareth, and he lived under their authority. His mother kept all these things safe in her heart.

And Jesus advanced in wisdom and in stature, and in favor with God and with people.

fields.title: Luke 3
fields.body_html:
The word of God comes to John

It was the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea; Herod ruled Galilee as tetrarch, his brother Philip ruled the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias ruled Abilene. Annas and Caiaphas held the high priesthood. In that year the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness. He went through all the country around the Jordan, announcing a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. It was as it stands written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: “A voice is calling out in the wilderness, ‘Get the road ready for the Lord, make the paths straight for him.’ Every valley will be filled in, and every mountain and hill brought low; the winding roads will be made straight, and the rough roads level, and all people will see the salvation of God.’”

Fruit that shows repentance

So John would say to the crowds who came out to be baptized by him, “You children of snakes! Who told you to run from the anger that is coming? Then bear fruit that fits your repentance. And do not start telling yourselves, ‘Abraham is our father.’ I tell you, God can raise up children for Abraham out of these stones. The ax is already lying at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.”

The crowds asked him, “Then what are we to do?” He answered them, “Whoever has two shirts must share with the person who has none, and whoever has food must do the same.” Tax collectors too came to be baptized. “Teacher,” they said to him, “what are we to do?” He told them, “Take no more than the amount you have been ordered to collect.” Some soldiers asked him too, “And what about us? What are we to do?” He told them, “Do not shake anyone down for money or make false charges, and be satisfied with your pay.”

One stronger than John is coming

The people were full of expectation, and all of them were asking themselves whether John might be the Christ. John answered them all, “I baptize you with water. But someone stronger than I am is coming, and I am not fit to untie the strap of his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn. But the chaff he will burn in a fire that never goes out.”

With many other words of appeal, John announced the good news to the people. But John had rebuked Herod the tetrarch for taking Herodias, his brother’s wife, and for all the other evil things he had done. So Herod added this to all the rest: he locked John up in prison.

The Spirit comes down on Jesus

At the time when all the people were being baptized, Jesus also received baptism. As he prayed, heaven opened, and the Holy Spirit came down on him in bodily form, like a dove. And a voice came from heaven: “You are my dear Son; you bring my heart delight.”

The family line of Jesus, back to Adam

Jesus was about thirty years old when he began his work. He was the son, as people supposed, of Joseph, son of Heli, son of Matthat, son of Levi, son of Melchi, son of Jannai, son of Joseph, son of Mattathias, son of Amos, son of Nahum, son of Esli, son of Naggai, son of Maath, son of Mattathias, son of Semein, son of Josech, son of Joda, son of Joanan, son of Rhesa, son of Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, son of Neri, son of Melchi, son of Addi, son of Cosam, son of Elmadam, son of Er, son of Joshua, son of Eliezer, son of Jorim, son of Matthat, son of Levi, son of Simeon, son of Judah, son of Joseph, son of Jonam, son of Eliakim, son of Melea, son of Menna, son of Mattatha, son of Nathan, son of David, son of Jesse, son of Obed, son of Boaz, son of Sala, son of Nahshon, son of Amminadab, son of Admin, son of Arni, son of Hezron, son of Perez, son of Judah, son of Jacob, son of Isaac, son of Abraham, son of Terah, son of Nahor, son of Serug, son of Reu, son of Peleg, son of Eber, son of Shelah, son of Cainan, son of Arphaxad, son of Shem, son of Noah, son of Lamech, son of Methuselah, son of Enoch, son of Jared, son of Mahalalel, son of Cainan, son of Enosh, son of Seth, son of Adam, son of God.

fields.title: Luke 4
fields.body_html:
The devil tests Jesus in the wilderness

Jesus came back from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit, and the Spirit led him through the wilderness for forty days, while the devil put him to the test. He went without food the whole time, and when the days were over, he was hungry. The devil said to him, “If you are the Son of God, order this stone to turn into bread.” Jesus answered him, “It stands written, ‘A person does not live on bread alone.’”

Then the devil took him up high, and in a single instant he let him see every kingdom of the world. And the devil said to him, “I will give you power over all of them, and all their glory. It has been handed over to me, and I hand it on to whoever I please. So if you will bow down to me in worship, all of it will belong to you.” Jesus answered him, “It stands written, ‘Worship the Lord your God, and serve no one but him.’”

Next the devil brought him to Jerusalem and set him on the high corner of the temple. “If you are the Son of God,” he told him, “jump down from here. For Scripture says, ‘He will give his angels orders about you, to keep you safe,’ and, ‘They will hold you up in their hands, so that your foot will not strike a stone.’” Jesus answered him, “It has been said, ‘You must not test the Lord your God.’” Once the devil had tried every kind of test, he left him to wait for a better moment.

Teaching in Galilee

Jesus went back to Galilee, and the power of the Spirit was with him. Word about him went out through all the country around. He kept teaching in their synagogues, and all who heard him gave him praise.

Jesus reads Isaiah in Nazareth

Then he came to Nazareth, the town where he grew up. On the Sabbath he went to the synagogue, as he always did, and stood up to read the Scriptures. Someone handed him the scroll of the prophet Isaiah. He opened it out and found the passage that says: “The Spirit of the Lord rests on me, for he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. He has sent me to announce freedom to the captives and sight to the blind, to set the downtrodden free, and to announce the year when the Lord shows favor.” He rolled the scroll up again, handed it back to the attendant, and took his seat. All the eyes in the synagogue were fixed on him. He began by telling them, “Today, as you have been listening, these words of Scripture have come true.” Everyone there was speaking in his favor, and they wondered at the words of grace that came from his mouth. And they kept saying, “Is this not Joseph’s son?” He said to them, “No doubt you will quote this saying to me: ‘Doctor, cure yourself!’ And you will tell me, ‘Do here in your own town the things we heard you did in Capernaum.’” He added, “Truly I tell you, a prophet is never welcome in his own hometown. But I tell you in truth: in Elijah’s day, when the sky stayed shut for three years and six months and a great famine struck the whole land, Israel had many widows. Yet Elijah was not sent to any of them, but to a widow at Zarephath in the land of Sidon. And in the time of the prophet Elisha Israel had many people with leprosy, yet not one of them was made clean except Naaman, a man from Syria.” When they heard this, everyone in the synagogue was filled with fury. They rose up and threw him out of the town. They led him to the edge of the hill where their town stood, meaning to hurl him down from there. But he passed through the middle of them and went away.

An unclean spirit driven out at Capernaum

Then he went down to the Galilean town of Capernaum. There he would teach the people on the Sabbath. His teaching left them astounded, for there was authority in what he said. In the synagogue was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he shouted with a loud voice, “Ah! What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God!” Jesus gave it a stern command: “Be quiet! Come out of him!” The demon hurled the man down in the middle of the room, then left him, and he was not hurt at all. Amazement came over everyone. “What is this message?” they asked one another. “He gives commands to the unclean spirits with authority and power, and out they go!” And talk about him spread to every place in the region around.

Simon’s mother-in-law healed

From the synagogue Jesus went to Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was in the grip of a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. He stood over her and commanded the fever to leave, and it left her. Immediately she got up and started looking after them.

Many healed at sunset

As the sun went down, all who had people at home sick with one disease or another brought them to him. He put his hands on each one and made them well. Demons also left many people, crying out, “You are the Son of God!” He silenced them with a rebuke and did not let them talk, for they knew he was the Christ.

Good news for the other towns

When day came, he went out to a deserted place. But the crowds went searching for him. They found him and tried to hold on to him so that he would not go away from them. But he told them, “I have to bring the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well. This is what I was sent to do.” And he continued to proclaim his message in the synagogues of Judea.

fields.title: Luke 5
fields.body_html:
The great catch of fish and the call of Simon

Once, as Jesus stood beside the lake of Gennesaret, the crowd was pushing in around him to hear the word of God. He noticed two boats drawn up at the edge of the lake. The fishermen had climbed out of them and were washing their nets. He got into one of the boats, the one that belonged to Simon, and asked him to push off a short way from the shore. Then he sat down and taught the crowds from the boat. When he had finished speaking, he told Simon, “Take the boat out where the water is deep, and lower your nets to catch fish.” Simon replied, “Master, we worked hard the whole night through and caught nothing. But on your word I will lower the nets.” So they did this, and they closed their nets around a great mass of fish. Their nets were starting to tear. They waved to their partners in the other boat to come over and lend a hand. The partners came, and together they loaded both boats with fish until the boats were starting to go under. When Simon Peter saw this, he threw himself down at Jesus’s knees and said, “Lord, leave me! I am a man full of sin.” He said this because the haul of fish they had brought in had left him stunned, and all who were with him as well. Zebedee’s sons, James and John, Simon’s partners, were stunned in the same way. “Do not be afraid,” Jesus told Simon. “From now on you will be catching people.” Once the boats were on land, they walked away from everything and followed him.

Jesus makes a man with leprosy clean

In one of the towns where Jesus was, there was a man covered all over with leprosy. Seeing Jesus, he fell face down and pleaded with him, “Lord, you can make me clean, if you choose to.” He stretched out his hand and laid it on the man. “I do want to,” he said. “Be made clean.” The leprosy left him that very moment. Jesus gave him strict orders not to tell anyone. “Instead,” he said, “go and let the priest examine you. Then bring the offering Moses ordered for your cleansing, as evidence to them.” But word about Jesus went out farther than ever. Large crowds kept gathering to listen and to be healed of their illnesses. Yet he kept slipping away to places in the wilderness to pray.

Authority on earth to forgive sins

On one of those days, while he was teaching, some Pharisees and teachers of the law were seated there. They had come from all the villages of Galilee, from Judea, and from Jerusalem. The power of the Lord was present for him to heal. Just then some men arrived with a paralyzed man lying on a bed. They wanted to carry him in and lay him in front of Jesus. The crowd left them no way of getting him in. So they climbed up on the roof, took away some of the tiles, and let him down on his bed into the middle of everyone, in front of Jesus. Jesus saw their faith and said, “My friend, your sins stand forgiven.” The scribes and Pharisees started to debate among themselves: “Who is this man, speaking blasphemy like this? Who has the power to forgive sins? Only God!” Jesus was aware of what was going through their minds, and he replied, “Why do you debate this in your hearts? Which is easier to say: ‘Your sins stand forgiven,’ or ‘Get up and walk’? But to show you that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,” he said to the paralyzed man, “I tell you, stand up, take your bed, and go off to your house.” Right away the man stood up in front of them, picked up the bed he had been lying on, and went home giving glory to God. Everyone was overcome with amazement. They glorified God, and full of awe they said, “What we have seen today is beyond belief!”

Levi leaves his tax booth

Later, Jesus went out and caught sight of a tax collector named Levi, seated at the place where he collected taxes. Jesus told him, “Follow me.” He stood up, left it all, and began following him.

Eating with tax collectors and sinners

Levi then gave a large feast at his house in honor of Jesus. A big crowd of tax collectors and other people were guests at the table with them. This made the Pharisees and their own scribes grumble. They said to his disciples, “How can you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” “People who are well have no use for a doctor,” Jesus answered them, “but people who are ill do. The reason I have come is to call sinners to repentance, not the righteous.”

Bridegroom, patches and wineskins

Then they said to him, “John’s disciples fast frequently and offer prayers, and the Pharisees’ disciples do the same. Yours, though, keep eating and drinking.” He answered them, “Would you make the guests at a wedding fast while the bridegroom is still among them? Days are coming, though, when the bridegroom will be taken away from them. Then, in those days, they will fast.” He told them a parable as well: “Nobody cuts a patch out of a new coat to sew on an old one. If anyone did, the new coat would be ruined, and the patch from the new would not suit the old coat either. Nor does anyone store new wine in old wineskins. That would make the skins split open; the new wine would spill, and the skins would be lost. Instead, new wine has to be put into fresh skins. And nobody who has been drinking old wine wants the new. ‘The old is good,’ they say.”

fields.title: Luke 6
fields.body_html:
Grain picked on the Sabbath

On a Sabbath Jesus was walking through fields of grain. His disciples were pulling off heads of grain, rubbing them between their hands, and eating them. Some of the Pharisees said, “Why are you doing something the law forbids on the Sabbath?” Jesus answered them, “Have you not even read about what David did when he and the men with him were hungry? He went into the house of God, took the bread set out before God, and ate it, and he gave some to the men with him. Yet the law allows no one but the priests to eat that bread.” And he told them, “The Son of Man is Lord over the Sabbath.”

A withered hand healed on the Sabbath

Another Sabbath came, and Jesus went into the synagogue and taught there. A man was present whose right hand was withered. The scribes and the Pharisees kept a close watch on him to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they could find a charge to bring against him. He knew their thoughts, though, and said to the man with the withered hand, “Get up and come stand in the middle.” The man rose and stood there. Then Jesus said to them, “Let me put a question to you: on the Sabbath, does the law allow doing good, or doing harm? Saving a life, or destroying it?” Jesus looked around at every one of them. Then he said to the man, “Hold out your hand.” The man did, and his hand was made healthy again. This filled them with mindless rage, and they talked together about what they could do to Jesus.

Jesus chooses the twelve

During those days Jesus went off to the mountain to pray, and he stayed up all night in prayer to God. At daybreak he summoned his disciples and picked out twelve of them, giving them the name apostles. They were Simon, to whom he gave the name Peter, and Simon’s brother Andrew; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew; Matthew and Thomas; James son of Alphaeus, and Simon, known as the Zealot; Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, the one who turned traitor.

Crowds come to hear and be healed

Coming down the mountain with them, Jesus stood on a flat stretch of ground. A big crowd of his disciples had gathered there, along with a huge number of people who had come from every part of Judea, from Jerusalem, and from the seacoast near Tyre and Sidon. They came to listen to him and to be cured of their illnesses, and people tormented by unclean spirits were made well. Everyone in the crowd kept trying to touch him, since power flowed out from him and healed every one of them.

The poor are blessed, the rich warned

Then, with his eyes on his disciples, he said, “Blessed are you poor, for the kingdom of God is yours. Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you will eat your fill. Blessed are those of you who are in tears now, for you will laugh.

Blessed are you when people hate you and push you out of their company, when they insult you and throw out your name as something evil, all because of the Son of Man. Be glad when that day comes, and jump for joy, because a great reward is waiting for you in heaven. Their ancestors did the very same things to the prophets. But how terrible for you who are rich, because you already have your comfort in full. How terrible for you who have eaten your fill now, because you will know hunger. How terrible for you who are laughing now, because you will grieve and cry.

How terrible for you when all people praise you! Their ancestors did just the same for the false prophets.

Love your enemies

But to you who are listening I say this: love your enemies. Treat those who hate you well. Speak blessings on those who curse you, and pray for those who treat you badly. If anyone strikes you on the cheek, present the other one as well. If anyone takes your coat, let them have your shirt too. Keep giving to everyone who asks you for something, and if anyone takes what is yours, do not ask for it back. However you want people to treat you, treat them the same way.

If you love those who love you, what thanks do you deserve? After all, sinners too love those who love them back. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what thanks do you deserve? Even sinners do as much. And if you lend to people you expect to pay you back, what thanks do you deserve? Sinners also lend to sinners, so as to get back as much again. Instead, love your enemies, treat them well, and lend without hoping to get anything back. Then you will receive a great reward, and you will be children of the Most High, since he is good to the thankless and the wicked. Show compassion, as your Father shows compassion. Do not sit in judgment on others, and you will never be judged. Do not pass sentence on them, and no sentence will be passed on you. Pardon others, and you will be pardoned. Give, and gifts will come to you: a full measure, packed down, shaken to settle it, and spilling over the top, will be poured into the fold of your robe. The measure you use for others is the measure that will be used for you.”

Blind guides, splinters and beams

He also told them a parable: “Can one blind person be a guide to another? Both of them will end up in a ditch, will they not? No disciple ranks above the teacher, but every disciple who is fully trained will become like the teacher. Why do you stare at the splinter in the eye of your brother or sister, and fail to notice the wooden beam in your own? How can you tell your brother or sister, ‘Brother or sister, here, let me get that splinter out of your eye,’ when you cannot see the beam in your own eye? You hypocrite! Get the beam out of your own eye first. Then you will see well enough to remove the splinter from the eye of your brother or sister.

Known by the fruit

For a sound tree does not yield rotten fruit, and a rotten tree does not yield sound fruit either. You can tell every tree by its own fruit. No one gathers figs from thorn plants or picks grapes off a bramble bush. From the good treasure in their heart, a good person produces what is good, and from what is evil, an evil person produces what is evil. For the mouth speaks out of what overflows the heart.

Building on rock

Why do you keep calling me ‘Lord, Lord’ when you do not do what I tell you? Let me show you what someone is like who comes to me, listens to my words, and acts on them. That person is like someone building a house, who dug, went down deep, and laid the foundation on the bedrock. When a flood came, the river crashed against that house but did not have the strength to shake it, because it had been built well. But whoever hears and does not act is like someone who built a house on the bare ground with no foundation. The river crashed against it, and at once it fell in, and that house was utterly destroyed.”

fields.title: Luke 7
fields.body_html:
A centurion’s servant is healed

When Jesus had finished saying all these things to the people who were listening, he went into Capernaum.

There was a centurion whose servant was very dear to him, and the servant was ill and close to death. He heard about Jesus and sent some Jewish elders to him, to ask him to come and save his servant’s life. They came to Jesus and pleaded with him urgently. “He deserves to have you do this for him,” they said. “He loves our people, and he is the one who built our synagogue for us.” So Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to say to him, “Lord, do not put yourself to any trouble. I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. That is why I did not think myself fit to come to you myself. Only speak a command, and let my servant be healed. For I myself serve under men who have authority over me, and I have soldiers under my command. I say to one, ‘Go!’ and off he goes; to another, ‘Come here!’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this!’ and he does it.” When Jesus heard this, he was amazed at the man. Turning to the crowd that followed him, he said, “I tell you, I have not found faith this great even in Israel.” When the messengers went back to the house, they found the servant well.

The widow’s son at Nain

Soon afterward Jesus went to a town called Nain. His disciples went with him, and so did a large crowd. As he came near the town gate, a dead man was being carried out. He was his mother’s only son, and she was a widow. A large crowd from the town was with her. When the Lord saw her, pity for her moved him deeply, and he said to her, “Stop weeping.” Then he went up and touched the bier, and the men carrying it stood still. He said, “Young man, I tell you, get up!” The dead man sat up and began to talk, and Jesus gave him back to his mother. Awe took hold of everyone, and they gave glory to God. “A great prophet has appeared among us!” they said, and, “God has come to help his people!” This news about him spread through all Judea and the whole region around it.

John asks about the one who is to come

John’s disciples told him about all these things. So John called two of his disciples and sent them to the Lord to ask, “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to look for someone else?” When the men reached him, they said, “John the Baptist sent us to you to ask, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or are we to look for someone else?’” Just then he healed many people of diseases, painful illnesses and evil spirits, and he gave many blind people the gift of sight. So he answered them, “Go back and tell John what you have seen and heard. The blind see again, the lame walk, people with leprosy are made clean, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor hear the good news. And blessed is anyone who does not find in me a reason to fall away.”

Jesus speaks about John

After John’s messengers had gone, Jesus began to talk to the crowds about John. “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swaying in the wind? If not, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft, fine clothes? Those who wear splendid clothes and live in luxury are found in the palaces of kings. Then what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and far more than a prophet. He is the one of whom Scripture says, ‘I am sending my messenger to go before you; he will make your road ready ahead of you.’ I tell you, of all who have been born of women, there is none greater than John. Yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he is.” All the people who heard this, even the tax collectors, agreed that God was in the right, because they had been baptized with John’s baptism. But the Pharisees and the experts in the law refused what God intended for them, since they had not let John baptize them.

Jesus went on, “Then how shall I picture the people of this generation? What are they like? They are like small children who sit in the town square and shout to each other, ‘We played wedding music on the flute for you, and you would not dance. We sang a funeral song, and you would not cry.’ For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘There is a demon in him.’ The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at the man! He is greedy for food and a heavy drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is shown to be right by all who are her children.”

The woman with the alabaster flask

One of the Pharisees invited Jesus to a meal with him. So he went into the Pharisee’s house and took his place at the table. Now there was a woman in the town who was a sinner. When she found out that Jesus was at table in the Pharisee’s house, she came with an alabaster flask of perfume. She stood behind him, at his feet, crying, and began to wet his feet with her tears. She dried them with the hair of her head, and she kissed his feet over and over and anointed them with the perfume. The Pharisee who had invited him saw this and said to himself, “This man, if he were a prophet, would have known who this woman is who is touching him, and what sort of woman she is: a sinner.” Jesus answered him, “Simon, there is something I want to tell you.” “Say it, Teacher,” he replied. Jesus said, “A moneylender had two men who owed him money. One owed him 500 denarii, and the other fifty. Neither of them could pay him back, so he freely canceled the debts of both. So which of the two will love him more?” Simon answered, “I would think the one whose larger debt he canceled.” Jesus said to him, “Your judgment is right.” Then he turned toward the woman and said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? When I came into your house, you gave me no water to wash my feet. But she has made my feet wet with her tears and dried them with her hair. You did not welcome me with a kiss. But ever since I came in, she has kept on kissing my feet. You did not anoint my head with olive oil, but she has anointed my feet with costly perfume. So I tell you, her sins, many as they are, stand forgiven; that is why she has shown so much love. But someone who is forgiven little loves little.” Then he said to her, “Your sins stand forgiven.” The others at the table with him began to say to one another, “Who is this man, that he even forgives sins?” But Jesus said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”

fields.title: Luke 8
fields.body_html:
Women who traveled with Jesus

Soon afterward Jesus went on through one town and village after another, preaching and announcing the good news of the kingdom of God. The twelve were with him, and so were some women who had been healed of evil spirits and diseases: Mary, called Magdalene, out of whom seven demons had gone; Joanna, the wife of Herod’s steward Chuza; Susanna; and many others. These women were using their own resources to provide for them.

Seed scattered on four kinds of ground

A large crowd was gathering, and people from town after town kept coming to him. He told them a parable: “A sower went out to scatter his seed. As he sowed, some of the seed dropped beside the road, where it was stepped on, and the birds swallowed it up. Other seed fell on the rock, and as soon as it sprouted it shriveled, because the ground held no moisture. Other seed landed among thornbushes, which sprang up with it and smothered it. And other seed dropped into good soil, sprang up, and produced a hundredfold harvest.” As he said this, he called out, “Whoever has ears to hear should listen!”

Why Jesus speaks in parables

His disciples asked him what this parable meant. He said, “You have been allowed to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but the others receive them in parables, so that they look but do not see, and listen but do not understand.

This is what the parable means: the seed is the word of God. Those beside the road are people who have heard, but then the devil comes and snatches the word out of their hearts, to keep them from believing and being saved. Those on the rock are people who welcome the word with joy when they hear it, but they have no root. They believe for a season, and when testing comes, they turn away. As for the seed that fell among thorns, these are people who hear, but as they go through life, the worries, wealth and pleasures of living choke them, so that their fruit never ripens. As for the seed in the good soil, these are people with a good and upright heart. They hear the word, hold on to it, and through endurance bear fruit.

A lamp set where it can be seen

Nobody who has lit a lamp then covers it with a bowl or tucks it under a bed. A lamp goes on a lampstand, where those who enter can see its light. Whatever is hidden will be shown plainly, and whatever is kept secret will surely be known and brought to light. So pay attention to how you listen. Those who have will receive more. Those who do not have will lose even what they seem to have.”

Those who hear and do God’s word

His mother and his brothers came to him, but the crowd kept them from getting to him. Someone told him, “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, and they want to see you.” But he answered them, “Those who hear the word of God and do what it says are my mother and my brothers.”

Jesus commands the wind and the water

One day Jesus got into a boat with his disciples and said to them, “Let us cross over to the far side of the lake.” So they put out from shore. While they were sailing, he fell asleep. A fierce windstorm swept down on the lake. Water was filling the boat, and they were in danger. They went and roused him, crying out, “Master, Master, we are lost!” He stood up and gave a stern order to the wind and the churning water. They stopped, and the lake became calm. Then he asked them, “Where is your faith?” Filled with fear and wonder, they asked one another, “Who is this, then, that the winds and the water obey when he gives the order?” They put in at the land of the Gerasenes, on the shore facing Galilee. As Jesus stepped onto the shore, a man from the town came toward him. He had demons in him, and for a long time he had gone without clothes and had lived, not in a house, but among the tombs. When the man saw Jesus, he screamed and threw himself down before him. In a loud voice he said, “What business do you have with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me!” For he had been ordering the unclean spirit to leave the man. Again and again it had taken hold of him. People kept him under guard and bound him with chains and fetters, but he would break the bonds, and the demon would drive him out into the wilderness. Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He said, “Legion”; for a great number of demons had entered him. The demons kept pleading with him not to command them to depart into the abyss.

Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the mountainside. The demons begged him for permission to enter those pigs, and he allowed them to. The demons left the man and went into the pigs. Then the whole herd stampeded down the cliff into the lake and drowned.

When the herders saw what had happened, they ran off and spread the news in the town and on the farms. People came out to see what had taken place. When they reached Jesus, they found the man whom the demons had left sitting at the feet of Jesus, wearing clothes and thinking clearly. And they were frightened. Those who had seen it told them how the man who had been under the power of demons had been made well. Then the whole population of the Gerasene region asked him to leave them, because a great fear had taken hold of them. So he got into the boat and went back. The man the demons had left kept begging to go with him, but Jesus sent him away and said, “Go back home and tell the story of everything God has done for you.” He went away and made known throughout the whole town everything Jesus had done for him.

A dying girl and a woman who touched Jesus

When Jesus came back across the lake, the people gave him a warm welcome, for they had all been waiting for him. Then a man named Jairus came. He was a ruler of the synagogue. Throwing himself down at the feet of Jesus, he begged him to come to his home, because his only child, a daughter about twelve years old, lay dying.

As he made his way there, the crowds were jammed tightly around him. Among them was a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years. She had spent everything she had on doctors, but none of them could cure her. Coming up behind Jesus, she touched the tassel on his cloak, and her bleeding stopped at once. Jesus asked, “Who touched me?” Everyone denied it, and Peter said, “Master, the crowds are hemming you in and pushing against you!” But Jesus said, “Someone did touch me. I felt power go out from me.” Realizing that she had been found out, the woman came forward, shaking, and threw herself down before him. With all the people listening, she explained her reason for touching him and told how she had been healed on the spot. Jesus said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace.”

Jesus was still speaking when a messenger arrived from the synagogue ruler’s house with the news, “Your daughter has died. There is no need to trouble the Teacher any further.” But Jesus heard it and answered Jairus, “Do not give way to fear. Only believe, and she will be made well.” Arriving at the house, he allowed only Peter, John and James, and the girl’s father and mother, to go in with him. Everyone was crying and wailing for her. But he told them, “Do not weep. She has not died. She is sleeping.” They ridiculed him, since they knew that she had died. But he took hold of her hand and called, “Child, get up!” Her spirit came back to her, and she rose at once, and he gave orders that she be given food. Her parents were beside themselves with amazement. But he charged them to keep what had happened to themselves.

fields.title: Luke 9
fields.body_html:
The Twelve sent out with power

Jesus called the Twelve together and gave them power and authority over every demon, and to cure diseases. He sent them out to announce the kingdom of God and to heal those who were ill. He told them, “Carry nothing with you for the road: no walking stick, no traveler’s bag, no bread, no money. And none of you is to have two tunics. Whatever house you go into, stay there, and leave the town from there. If any do not welcome you, then as you leave that town, shake its dust off your feet. That will be evidence against them.” So they set out and went from village to village, bringing the good news and healing people everywhere.

Herod hears about Jesus

Herod the tetrarch heard about everything that was taking place, and he did not know what to make of it. Some people were saying that John had been raised from the dead; some, that Elijah had appeared; and others, that one of the prophets from long ago had risen again. But Herod said, “I cut off John’s head myself. Who, then, is this man I keep hearing such things about?” And he kept trying to see him.

Bread for five thousand

The apostles came back and gave him an account of everything they had done. He took them with him and slipped away privately to a town called Bethsaida. But the crowds found out and followed him. He welcomed them and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and he cured those who needed to be healed.

As the day was ending, the Twelve came to him. “Dismiss the crowd,” they said. “Then they can go to the villages and farms around here and find somewhere to stay and something to eat. This is a lonely place.” But he said to them, “Give them something to eat yourselves.” They answered, “We have nothing but five loaves of bread and two fish, unless we go and buy food ourselves for this whole crowd.” There were about five thousand men there. He told his disciples, “Get them to sit down in groups of fifty or so.” They did this, and everyone sat down. He took the five loaves and the two fish, looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. He broke them and kept handing them to the disciples to serve to the crowd. Everyone ate and had plenty. Then what they had left was gathered up: twelve baskets full of broken pieces.

Peter says who Jesus is

One time Jesus was praying in a quiet place, and only the disciples were with him. He asked them, “Who do the people in the crowds say I am?” They replied, “John the Baptist. Others say Elijah. Others say that one of the prophets of long ago has risen again.” Then he asked them, “But what about you? Who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “You are God’s Christ.”

He gave them strict orders not to tell this to anyone. “The Son of Man has to suffer a great deal,” he said. “The elders, the chief priests and the scribes will reject him. He will be put to death, and on the third day he will be raised.”

Taking up the cross every day

Then he said to everyone, “Anyone who wants to come after me must say no to themselves, pick up their cross every day, and keep following me. Anyone who sets out to save their own life will lose it. But anyone who loses their life because of me will save it. Suppose someone wins the whole world but is ruined and loses themselves. What has that person gained? If anyone is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of that person when he comes in his own glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. I tell you truly: among those standing here are some who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God.”

Jesus is changed on the mountain

Some eight days after these words, Jesus went up the mountain to pray, taking Peter, John and James along. While he prayed, the look of his face was changed, and his clothes turned white and flashed like lightning. Suddenly two men were talking with him: Moses and Elijah. They appeared in glory and were speaking of his departure, the exodus he was about to complete in Jerusalem. Peter and the others with him had been overcome by sleep. But when they were wide awake, they saw his glory, and the two men who stood beside him. When the two men were about to part from him, Peter spoke up: “Master, it is good that we are here. We should set up three tents, one for you, one for Moses, one for Elijah.” Peter did not really know what he was saying. While Peter was still speaking, a cloud came and cast its shadow over them, and they were frightened as they went into the cloud. Then a voice came from the cloud: “This is my Son, the Chosen One. Listen to him.” When the voice had finished, Jesus was there alone. The disciples kept quiet. At that time they said nothing to anyone about the things they had seen.

A father’s only son is set free

On the following day, after they had come down the mountain, a big crowd was there to meet him. A man in the crowd shouted, “Teacher, I beg you, look at my son! He is my only child. A spirit grabs him, and suddenly he shrieks. It shakes him violently until he foams at the mouth, and it will hardly let him go; it leaves him battered. I pleaded with your disciples to drive it out, but they did not have the power.” Jesus replied, “Oh, this generation, with no faith and so twisted! How long must I be with you and put up with you? Bring your son here.” The boy was still on his way when the demon dashed him to the ground and shook him violently. But Jesus gave the unclean spirit a stern command. He healed the boy and returned him to his father. All the people were astounded at the majesty of God.

Jesus speaks again of being handed over

People were still wondering at everything he was doing when he said to his disciples, “Let these words sink deep into your ears: the Son of Man is going to be handed over into the hands of human beings.” They did not know what he meant by this. It had been veiled from them so that they would not see what it meant. And they were afraid to ask him about what he had said.

Who is the greatest

A dispute came up among them: which of them was the greatest? Jesus knew what they were thinking in their hearts. He took a child and had the child stand beside him. Then he said to them, “Anyone who receives this child in my name is receiving me. And anyone who receives me is receiving the one who sent me. For whoever is least among all of you, that is the one who is great.”

Not against you, but for you

John responded, “Master, we saw a man driving out demons by using your name, and we kept telling him to stop, because he is not a follower along with us.” Jesus told him, “Do not try to stop him. Anyone who is not against you is on your side.”

A Samaritan village turns Jesus away

As the time drew near for him to be taken up, he turned his face toward Jerusalem, determined to go there. He sent messengers on ahead of him. On their way they went into a village of the Samaritans to make arrangements for him. But the people there refused to welcome him, since his face was turned toward Jerusalem. Seeing this, the disciples James and John said, “Lord, is it your wish that we command fire to come down from heaven and burn them up?” But Jesus turned and gave them a stern rebuke. And they went on to a different village.

Would-be followers on the road

While they were going along the road, someone told him, “Wherever you go, I will follow you.” Jesus said to him, “Foxes have their holes, and the birds in the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay down his head.” To another man he said, “Follow me.” But the man replied, “Lord, allow me to go first and bury my father.” Jesus told him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead. As for you, go and spread the news of the kingdom of God everywhere.” Yet another said, “I will follow you, Lord, but allow me first to take leave of the people at my home.” Jesus answered, “No one who sets a hand to the plow and keeps looking back is suited for the kingdom of God.”

fields.title: Luke 10
fields.body_html:
Seventy-two sent ahead in pairs

After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others as well. He sent them out in pairs ahead of him, to every town and place he was going to visit. He told them, “There is a great harvest, but only a few workers. So plead with the Lord of the harvest to send workers out to bring in his harvest. Go on your way. I am sending you out like lambs among wolves. Take no money bag, no pack and no sandals, and do not stop to greet anyone on the way. Whatever house you go into, begin by saying, ‘Peace be on this household.’ If someone there is a person of peace, your peace will stay with that person. If not, it will come back to you. Stay in that one house, eating and drinking whatever they give you, since a worker has earned their pay. Do not keep changing from one house to another. Whenever a town takes you in, eat whatever food they put in front of you. Heal those in it who are sick, and tell the people, ‘The kingdom of God has drawn near to you.’ But if you go into a town where the people do not welcome you, go out into its streets and say, ‘Against you we wipe off even the dust of your town that has stuck to our feet. All the same, be sure of this: the kingdom of God has come near.’ I tell you, on that day Sodom will be better off than that town.

How terrible for you, Chorazin! How terrible for you, Bethsaida! If the mighty deeds that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, their people would long ago have sat down in sackcloth and ashes and repented. But at the judgment Tyre and Sidon will be better off than you. And you, Capernaum, will you be raised as high as heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades.

Anyone who listens to you listens to me. Anyone who turns you away turns me away, and anyone who turns me away turns away the one who sent me.”

The seventy-two come back rejoicing

The seventy-two came back full of joy. “Lord,” they said, “when we use your name, even the demons obey us!” He told them, “I watched Satan fall from heaven like a flash of lightning. I have given you authority to trample snakes and scorpions underfoot, and authority over all the enemy’s power. Nothing at all will be able to hurt you. But do not be glad because the spirits obey you. Be glad instead that your names stand written in heaven.”

Hidden from the wise, shown to little children

At that very time Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have kept these things hidden from the wise and the clever, and have made them known to little children. Yes, Father, for this is what seemed good to you. My Father has put all things into my hands. Who the Son is, only the Father knows; and who the Father is, only the Son knows, along with anyone to whom the Son is willing to make him known.”

Then he turned to the disciples and said to them alone, “Blessed are the eyes that are seeing what you see. I tell you, many prophets and kings longed to see the things you are seeing, yet never saw them; they longed to hear the things you are hearing, yet never heard them.”

Who is my neighbor?
