Then an expert in the law stood up to put Jesus to the test. “Teacher,” he said, “what do I have to do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus answered him, “What stands written in the law? What do you read there?” He answered, “‘You are to love the Lord your God with your whole heart, your whole soul, your whole strength and your whole mind,’ and ‘your neighbor as you love yourself.’” Jesus told him, “Your answer is right. Do this, and you will live.”

But the man wanted to show that he was in the right, so he asked Jesus, “And who counts as my neighbor?” Jesus took up the question and said, “A man was on his way down from Jerusalem to Jericho when robbers set on him. They tore off his clothes, gave him a beating, and went off and left him lying there half dead. It so happened that a priest was traveling down by that same road. He saw the man, but went past him, keeping to the far side. A Levite did the same. He came to the spot, saw him, and went past on the far side. Then a Samaritan, who was on a journey, came to where the man lay. When he saw him, his heart went out to him. He went over to him, poured oil and wine on his wounds and bound them up. Then he lifted him onto his own animal, took him to an inn, and looked after him. The next day he took out two denarii and handed them to the innkeeper. ‘Care for him,’ he said, ‘and if you spend anything more, I will pay you back on my return.’ Now which of these three, in your view, proved to be a neighbor to the man the robbers attacked?” He answered, “The one who was merciful to him.” Jesus told him, “You go, then, and do the same.”

Martha serves, Mary listens

As they went on their way, Jesus came into a village where a woman named Martha welcomed him as her guest. Martha had a sister, Mary, who sat down at Jesus’s feet and kept listening to his words. But Martha was being pulled in every direction by all the work of serving. She came up and said, “Lord, does it not matter to you that my sister has left me to do the serving on my own? So tell her to give me a hand.” The Lord answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are fretting and in a stir about so many things. Yet there is need of few things, or only of one. Mary has picked the good share, and it is not going to be taken from her.”

fields.title: Luke 11
fields.body_html:
Lord, teach us to pray

Once Jesus was praying in a certain place. When he had finished, one of his disciples asked him, “Lord, teach us how to pray, the way John taught his own disciples.” He said to them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, may your name be honored as holy. May your kingdom come. Each day give us the bread we need. Forgive us our sins, since we also forgive all who owe us. And do not bring us into temptation.’”

The friend at midnight

Then he said to them, “Imagine that one of you has a friend, and you go to his house in the middle of the night and say to him, ‘My friend, lend me three loaves. Another friend of mine has come to my house from a journey, and I have nothing to set out for him to eat.’ Would that friend call back from inside, ‘Do not trouble me. The door is already shut for the night, and my children are in bed with me. I cannot get up now to hand you anything’? I tell you, even if friendship is not enough to get him out of bed to give you the bread, your boldness in asking without shame will get him up, and he will give you as much as you need.

Ask, search, knock

So I tell you: ask, and God will give to you; search, and you will find; knock, and God will open the door for you. For all who ask receive, all who search find, and all who knock have the door opened to them. Is there a father among you who would hand his son a snake when the boy asked for a fish? Or if he asked for an egg, would he give him a scorpion? You are evil, and yet you know how to give your children good gifts. Then how much more will the Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!”

By the finger of God

Jesus was driving out a demon that had left a man unable to speak. Once the demon was gone, the man spoke. The crowds were amazed. But some of them said, “It is by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons, that he drives out the demons.” Others, wanting to test him, kept asking him for a sign from heaven. But he knew what they were thinking, and he said to them, “If a kingdom is torn apart by its own people, it is laid waste, and its houses fall one upon another. If Satan too is split against himself, how can his kingdom last? Yet that is what you are saying: that I drive out the demons by Beelzebul. And if I drive out the demons by Beelzebul, by whose power do your own people drive them out? So they themselves will be the ones to judge you. But suppose it is by God’s finger that I drive the demons out. Then the kingdom of God has already reached you. As long as a strong man keeps guard over his own palace with all his weapons, his goods are left in peace. But then a man stronger than he is comes against him and wins the fight. He strips away all the armor the strong man was counting on, and shares out the goods he has seized. Anyone who does not stand with me stands against me, and anyone who does not help me gather is scattering.

The unclean spirit returns

When an unclean spirit has left a person, it wanders through dry, empty places looking for a place to rest. When it finds none, it says, ‘I will go back to my house, where I came from.’ It arrives and finds the house swept and tidied. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they go in and make their home there. In the end that person is worse off than at the start.”

Hearing and keeping God’s word

While he was saying these things, a woman in the crowd called out to him, “Blessed is the woman who carried you in her womb and fed you at her breasts!” But he said, “Even more blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.”

Something greater than Jonah

With the crowds pressing in more and more, he began to say, “This generation is an evil one. It looks for a sign, yet the only sign it will be given is the sign of Jonah. For just as Jonah was a sign to the people of Nineveh, the Son of Man will be a sign to this generation. At the judgment the queen of the South will stand up with the people of this generation and condemn them, because she came from the far ends of the earth to listen to Solomon’s wisdom; and here is something greater than Solomon. At the judgment the people of Nineveh will stand up with this generation and condemn it, because they repented when Jonah preached; and here is something greater than Jonah.

Light within

A lamp, once lit, is not hidden away in a cellar or put under a basket; it is set on a lampstand, where anyone coming in will see its light. Your body’s lamp is your eye. If your eye is clear, light fills your whole body as well. If your eye is bad, darkness fills your body too. So be careful that the light inside you is not really darkness. So if light fills your whole body and no part of it is dark, it will be bright all through, as when a lamp shines on you with its beam.”

The inside of the cup

As he finished speaking, a Pharisee asked him to eat at his home, and he went in and took his place at the table. The Pharisee saw that he had not washed before the meal, and it surprised him. But the Lord said to him, “You Pharisees clean the cup and the dish on the outside, but your own insides are full of plunder and wickedness. Foolish people! The one who made the outside made the inside as well, did he not? Rather, give what is inside as gifts to the poor, and then everything is clean for you.

How terrible for you

But how terrible for you Pharisees! You set aside for God a tenth even of mint and rue and every kind of garden plant, yet you pass over justice and the love of God. Justice and love are what you should have practiced, while not neglecting the tenth. How terrible for you Pharisees! You love to sit in the front seats of the synagogues and to be greeted in the marketplaces. How terrible for you! You are like graves with no marker, and the people who walk over them are unaware of it.”

Loads too heavy to carry

One of the experts in the law responded to him, “Teacher, by saying this you are insulting us as well.” He said, “How terrible for you experts in the law too! You pile on people loads that are hard to carry, and you yourselves will not touch those loads with even one of your fingers. How terrible for you! You build monuments over the prophets’ graves, yet those prophets died at the hands of your ancestors. So you are witnesses, and you give your approval to what your ancestors did: they did the killing, and you do the building. That is why the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles. They will kill some of them and hunt down others.’ And so the blood of all the prophets shed since the world was founded will be charged to this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who died between the altar and the house of God. Yes, I tell you, this generation will be charged with it. How terrible for you experts in the law! You have carried off the key of knowledge. You have not gone in yourselves, and you have stood in the way of those who were going in.”

When he left that place, the scribes and the Pharisees turned bitterly against him and kept pressing him with questions about many things, watching for a chance to trap him by his own words.

fields.title: Luke 12
fields.body_html:
The leaven of the Pharisees

Meanwhile the crowd had grown to many thousands, so packed that people were stepping on one another. Jesus began to speak, first of all to his disciples: “Watch out for the yeast of the Pharisees. I mean their hypocrisy. Everything that is covered up now will be uncovered, and every secret will come out. So anything you said in the dark will be heard in broad daylight. Anything you spoke into someone’s ear in a back room will be announced from the tops of the houses.

The one to fear

My friends, I tell you this: do not be afraid of people who can kill the body but then can do nothing further. I will point out the one you should fear. Fear the one who, after the killing is done, has the right to throw you into hell. Yes, I tell you, he is the one to fear. You can buy five sparrows for two pennies, can you not? Yet God does not forget a single one of them. Why, every hair on your head has been counted. So do not be afraid. You matter more than a great many sparrows.

I tell you, if anyone openly stands with me in front of others, the Son of Man will stand with that person in front of God’s angels. But whoever denies knowing me in front of others will be denied in front of God’s angels. Anyone who says something against the Son of Man will be forgiven. But anyone who speaks evil against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. People will bring you before synagogues, rulers and officials. When they do, do not worry over how to answer the charges or what words to use. When the moment comes, the Holy Spirit will teach you what you need to say.”

A rich man and his barns

Someone in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to share our father’s property with me.” Jesus answered, “Friend, who made me your judge, or put me in charge of dividing your property?” Then he said to them, “Take care! Keep yourselves from every kind of greed. Even when someone has more than enough, life does not come from the things a person owns.” Then he told them a parable: “There was a rich man whose land gave a huge harvest. He kept turning it over in his mind: ‘What am I to do? I have no place where I can store my harvest.’ Then he said, ‘Here is my plan. I will pull down my barns and put up larger ones, and I will gather all my grain and my goods into them. Then I will say to myself, “You have plenty of good things put away for years to come. Rest now. Eat, drink, and have a good time.”‘ But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life is being asked back from you. And the things you have made ready, whose will they be then?’ That is how it is for anyone who piles up wealth for themselves but is not rich in God’s sight.”

Life is more than food

Then Jesus said to his disciples, “That is why I tell you: stop worrying about your life and what you will eat, or about your body and what you will put on it. Life is worth more than food, and the body is worth more than clothing. Think about the ravens. They do not plant or harvest. They have no storehouse and no barn. Yet God feeds them. And you are worth far more than birds! Which of you can make your life one hour longer by worrying? If you cannot manage even something so small, why worry about all the rest? Look at how the lilies grow. They do not work hard or spin thread. But I tell you, Solomon himself, in all his glory, never wore anything as fine as one of them. If God dresses the wild grass this way, grass that is in the field today and fuel for the oven tomorrow, he will do far more for you. How little faith you have! So do not be always looking for what you will eat and what you will drink, and do not be on edge about it. These are the things that the nations of the world chase after, but your Father knows that you need them. Instead, set your hearts on his kingdom, and you will receive these things besides.

Do not be afraid, my little flock. Your Father has gladly chosen to give you the kingdom. Sell what you own and give the money to people in need. Get yourselves money bags that never wear out, a treasure in heaven that will never run out. No thief can get near it there, and no moth can spoil it. Your heart will be wherever your treasure is.

Servants waiting for their master

Stay ready for work, with your belt tied and your lamp lit. Be like people who are waiting for their master to come home from a wedding feast, ready to open the door the moment he arrives and knocks. Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake and watching when he comes. Truly I tell you, he will tie on an apron, seat them at the table, and come and wait on them himself. He may come in the middle of the night or even later, but if he finds them ready, those servants are blessed.

You can be sure of this: if the owner of a house knew the hour when the thief was on his way, he would not let anyone dig through the walls of his house. Be ready yourselves, then. The Son of Man is coming at an hour when you do not think he will.”

Peter asked, “Lord, is this parable meant for us, or are you telling it to everyone?” The Lord answered, “Who, then, is the manager who can be trusted and who acts wisely? His master will put him in charge of the other workers in the household, to give them their share of food when it is due. Blessed is that servant if his master finds him doing just that when he comes home. I tell you truly, he will put him in charge of everything he owns. But that servant may think, ‘My master will be a long while yet.’ He may start beating the menservants and the serving girls, and eating and drinking until he is drunk. Then his master will arrive on a day the servant does not expect, at an hour he has not guessed. He will cut him to pieces and put him with the unfaithful. A servant who knew his master’s wishes but made no preparations and did not carry them out will receive a heavy beating. But a servant who did not know, though he did what deserved a beating, will get a lighter one. Much will be asked of everyone who has been given much. And when much has been put in someone’s care, even more will be asked of that person.

Fire on the earth

I came to set fire to the earth, and how I long for it to be blazing already! But first I must go through a baptism, and I am under great strain until it is over! Do you suppose that I came to bring peace to the earth? No, I tell you, I came to bring division. From now on, a family of five will be split, three against two and two against three. Father will turn against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, a woman against her son’s wife and the wife against her husband’s mother.”

Reading the time

Jesus also said to the crowds, “When you see a cloud coming up in the west, you say straight away, ‘There will be rain,’ and so there is. And when the south wind is blowing, you say, ‘A scorching day is coming,’ and so it turns out. You hypocrites! You can read the face of the earth and the sky. How is it, then, that you cannot read what this moment means? Why can you not decide for yourselves what is right? When someone is taking you to court before the magistrate, do your best to settle with them while you are still on the way. If you do not, your accuser may drag you before the judge. The judge may hand you over to the officer, and the officer may throw you into prison. I tell you, there will be no way out for you until the very last penny is paid.”

fields.title: Luke 13
fields.body_html:
Unless you repent

At that very time some people there told Jesus about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with the blood of their sacrifices. He answered them, “Do you suppose that these Galileans suffered this because they were worse sinners than all the other people of Galilee? No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you will all perish as they did. Or think of those eighteen who were killed when the tower at Siloam fell on them. Do you suppose they were more guilty than everyone else living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you will all perish just as they did.”

A fig tree with no fruit

Then he told this parable:

“A man had a fig tree growing in his vineyard. He came to look for fruit on it, but found none. So he said to the man who tended the vineyard, ‘Three years now I have come to this fig tree looking for fruit, and I never find any. Cut it down! Why should it keep wasting good ground?’ The man answered, ‘Sir, let it stand this year too, while I dig around it and work manure into the soil. If after that it bears fruit next year, well and good. If it does not, you can have it cut down.’”

A daughter of Abraham set free

Once, on a Sabbath, Jesus was teaching in one of the local synagogues. A woman was there whom a spirit had kept sick for eighteen years. Her back was bent, and she could not stand fully upright. When Jesus saw her, he called her over and told her, “Woman, you have been released from your illness.” Then he placed his hands on her, and right away she stood up straight and began to give glory to God. But the ruler of the synagogue was annoyed that Jesus had healed someone on the Sabbath, and he spoke up and told the crowd, “Work may be done on six days. Come to be healed on any of them, but not on the Sabbath day.” The Lord answered him, “You hypocrites! On the Sabbath every one of you unties your ox or your donkey from its stall and takes it out for water, do you not? And here is a daughter of Abraham whom Satan has kept tied up for eighteen whole years. Should she not be untied from this bond on the Sabbath day?” When he said this, everyone who had set themselves against him was put to shame, while the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things he was doing.

Like a mustard seed, like yeast

So he said, “What is the kingdom of God like? What picture shall I use for it? It is like this: a man took a mustard seed and sowed it in his own garden. It kept growing until it was a tree, and birds of the air came and nested among its branches.”

Once more he said, “With what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like yeast. A woman took some and hid it in about 40 pounds of flour, and in time the whole batch rose.”

Strive to enter

Jesus traveled on from town to town and village to village, teaching, and pressing on toward Jerusalem. Someone asked him, “Lord, is it only a few who are being saved?” He said to them, “Struggle hard to get in through the narrow door. Many people, I tell you, will look for a way in and will fail. When the master of the house has risen and locked the door, you will find yourselves outside. You will knock and call out, ‘Lord, open up for us!’ And his answer to you will be, ‘I do not know you; I do not know where you are from.’ Then you will begin to protest, ‘We ate and drank in your company, and it was in our streets that you taught!’ But he will tell you, ‘I do not know where you come from. Go away from me, all of you whose work is wrongdoing!’ You will weep there and grind your teeth when you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and every one of the prophets inside the kingdom of God, and yourselves driven out. And others will arrive from east and west, from north and south, and sit down to eat in the kingdom of God. Some who are last now will be first, and some who are first now will be last.”

A message for Herod

At that very time some Pharisees came up to him with a warning: “Get away from here and be on your way, because Herod intends to kill you.” He answered them, “Go and tell that fox: ‘Today and tomorrow I cast out demons and carry out cures, and on the third day I finish my course.’ But I must go on my way today, tomorrow, and the day after, because it cannot be that a prophet should die anywhere but in Jerusalem. Jerusalem, Jerusalem! You kill the prophets and stone the messengers sent to you. How many times I wanted to gather your children, the way a hen keeps her young ones under her wings! But you refused. Now your house is left to you. I tell you, you will not see me until the time comes when you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

fields.title: Luke 14
fields.body_html:
A Sabbath meal and a man with dropsy

One Sabbath he went to eat a meal at the house of one of the leading Pharisees, and the people there kept a close eye on him. There in front of him was a man whose body was swollen with dropsy. Jesus responded by asking the experts in the law and the Pharisees, “Does the law allow healing on the Sabbath, or does it not?” But they said nothing. So he took hold of the man, healed him, and sent him on his way. Then he said to them, “If one of you had a son or an ox that fell into a well on the Sabbath, would you not pull him out right away?” And they had no answer to give to this.

Taking the lowest place

When he saw how the guests were picking out the places of honor for themselves, he gave them a parable: “If you are invited to a wedding feast, do not settle yourself in the place of honor. Someone of higher rank than you may be among the guests, and the host who invited you both will come over and say, ‘Give your place to this guest.’ Then, to your shame, you will start down to the lowest place. No, when you are invited, go and take the last place at the table, so that when your host comes over he will tell you, ‘Friend, move further up.’ Then everyone eating with you will see the honor you are given. For everyone who lifts themselves up will be brought low, and the one who takes the low place will be lifted up.”

Guests who cannot repay

Then he said to his host as well, “When you put on a lunch or a dinner, do not ask your friends, your brothers and sisters, your relatives, or your wealthy neighbors. They might ask you back, and that would be your repayment. Instead, when you hold a feast, ask the poor to come, and those who are maimed, lame, or blind. And you will be blessed, for they have no way to pay you back. Your repayment will come at the resurrection of the righteous.”

The dinner the guests refused

One of the guests at the table heard this and said to him, “Blessed is anyone who will sit at the table in the kingdom of God!” He answered him, “Once a man was putting on a large dinner, and he had asked many people to it. When the hour of the dinner arrived, he sent his servant out to say to the guests he had asked, ‘Come, it is all ready now.’ But all of them alike began to ask to be excused. The first told him, ‘I have bought a piece of land, and I have to go out and look at it. I am asking you to excuse me.’ Another said, ‘I have bought five pairs of oxen, and I am on my way to test them. I am asking you to excuse me.’ And another said, ‘I have taken a wife, and that is why I am not able to come.’ The servant came back and told his master all of this. At that the owner of the house was angry, and he said to his servant, ‘Hurry out into the squares and alleys of the town, and bring the poor, the maimed, the blind, and the lame in here.’ Then the servant said, ‘Master, your order has been carried out, and there are still empty places.’ The master told the servant, ‘Go out to the country roads and the hedgerows, and press people to come in, so that my house will be full. For I tell you all, not a single one of the men I first invited will taste my dinner.’”

Counting the cost of following

Many crowds were walking along with him. He turned around and said to them, “No one can be my disciple who comes to me without hating their father and mother, their wife and children, their brothers and sisters, and even their own life. Unless a person carries their own cross and walks behind me, they cannot be my disciple. If any of you planned to build a tower, would you not sit down first and add up the expense, to find out whether you could afford to finish it? If you lay the foundation and cannot finish the job, everyone who sees it will start to make fun of you. They will say, ‘Here is someone who started to build and could not finish.’ Or what king sets out to fight another king without first sitting down to weigh whether his 10,000 troops can stand against an enemy who comes with 20,000? If he cannot, then while the other king is still a long way off, he will send envoys to ask how peace can be made. So it is with you: whoever does not let go of all that they have cannot be my disciple.

Salt that loses its taste

So salt is a good thing. But if even salt goes flat, how will its flavor be brought back? It is no use for the field, or even for the manure heap; people just throw it away. Whoever has ears to hear should listen!”

fields.title: Luke 15
fields.body_html:
One sheep out of a hundred

Tax collectors and sinners, all of them, kept coming near to listen to him. But the Pharisees and the scribes complained among themselves. “This man welcomes sinners,” they said, “and even shares meals with them.” So Jesus put this parable to them: “Which man among you, if he owned a hundred sheep and lost one of them, would not leave the ninety-nine out in the wild country and search for the lost one until he found it? And when he finds it, he hoists it onto his shoulders, delighted. Back at home, he invites his friends and neighbors over. ‘Celebrate with me,’ he tells them, ‘because the sheep I lost has been found.’ In the same way, I tell you, one sinner who repents will bring more joy in heaven than ninety-nine righteous people who have no need to repent.

A coin swept for and found

Or what woman with ten silver coins, if she lost one of them, would not light a lamp, sweep out her house and hunt for it carefully until she found it? When she finds it, she gathers her friends and neighbors. ‘Be glad with me,’ she says, ‘for the coin I had lost is found.’ So it is, I tell you: when one sinner repents, there is joy before the angels of God.”

A father and his two sons

Then he said, “A man had two sons. The younger son said to his father, ‘Father, let me have the part of the estate that will come to me.’ So the father split what he had between the two of them. Only a few days later the younger son packed up everything he owned and traveled to a far country, where he threw his property away on a reckless way of life. When he had used up everything, a terrible famine struck that whole land, and he began to go without. So he went and attached himself to one of the people of that country, and the man sent him out into his fields to look after pigs. He wished he could fill himself up with the carob pods the pigs were eating, but no one gave him a thing. At last he saw his situation clearly. ‘So many of my father’s hired workers have more bread than they can eat,’ he said, ‘while I am dying of hunger here! I will get up and go back to my father, and I will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I do not deserve to be called your son any longer. Take me on as one of your hired workers.”‘ So he set off and went back to his father. His father caught sight of him while he was still far away, and his heart went out to him. He ran to meet him, embraced him and kissed him warmly. His son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I do not deserve to be called your son any longer.’ But the father said to his servants, ‘Hurry! Bring out the finest robe and dress him in it. Give him a ring for his hand and sandals for his feet. Fetch the calf we have been fattening and slaughter it. Let us eat and celebrate, for my son here was dead, and now he lives again. He was lost, and now he has been found.’ And the celebration began.

The older son

All this time the older son had been out in the field. On his way back, as he came close to the house, the sound of music and dancing reached him. He called over one of the servants and asked him what this could mean. ‘Your brother is home,’ the servant told him, ‘and your father has slaughtered the fattened calf, because his son has come back to him alive and well.’ At this he grew angry and would not go inside. His father came out and appealed to him. He replied to his father, ‘Listen! For all these years I have worked like a slave for you. Not once have I gone against your orders. And not once have you given me a young goat for a feast with my friends. But this son of yours has eaten up your property with prostitutes, and the moment he turns up, you slaughter the fattened calf for him!’ His father answered, ‘My child, you are with me always, and all that is mine belongs to you. But it was only right to celebrate and rejoice, for this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.’”

fields.title: Luke 16
fields.body_html:
A manager who acted shrewdly

Jesus also told the disciples this: “A rich man had a manager, and word reached him that this man was squandering what he owned. So he sent for him and said, ‘What is this that I keep hearing about you? Hand in a report on how you have managed my affairs, because you cannot be my manager any longer.’ The manager thought it over: ‘My master is taking my position from me. What am I to do? Digging is too hard for me, and I would be ashamed to beg. Now I know what I will do, so that when I am put out of my job, people will open their homes to me.’ He sent for his master’s debtors one by one. To the first he said, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ ‘About 600 gallons of olive oil,’ he answered. The manager told him, ‘Here is your bill. Sit down quickly and write 300 gallons.’ Then he said to another, ‘And what do you owe?’ ‘About 600 bushels of wheat,’ he replied. The manager told him, ‘Take your bill and write about 500.’ So the master gave the dishonest manager credit for acting so shrewdly. For the people of this age deal more shrewdly with others of their own kind than the people of the light do. And I tell you, use the wealth of this unjust world to make friends for yourselves, so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into the eternal homes.

Someone who is faithful in the smallest matter is faithful in large matters too, and someone who is dishonest in the smallest matter is dishonest in large matters too. So if you have not been faithful in handling unjust wealth, who will put real wealth in your care? And if you have not proved faithful with what is another’s, who will hand you what is your own? No servant in a household can serve two masters. Either the servant will hate one master and love the other, or be loyal to one and look down on the other. You cannot serve both God and wealth.”

Lovers of money

The Pharisees were listening to all this. They loved money, and they turned up their noses at him. He said to them, “You are the ones who make yourselves out to be righteous in front of people, but God knows your hearts. What people think highly of is loathsome in God’s sight.

The law and the prophets lasted until John. From then on, the kingdom of God is announced as good news, and everyone is pressing their way into it.

Yet heaven and earth will pass away more easily than one tiny stroke of the law will fall away.

Any man who divorces his wife and marries someone else is committing adultery, and the man who marries a woman her husband has divorced is committing adultery too.

A rich man and a poor man named Lazarus

There was once a rich man who wore purple and fine linen and feasted in great style day after day. And a poor man named Lazarus had been put down at his gate. His body was covered with sores, and he longed to fill his stomach with whatever dropped from the rich man’s table. Instead, the dogs would come and lick his sores. The day came when the poor man died, and angels carried him off to be at Abraham’s side. The rich man also died, and was given a burial. From Hades, in the midst of his torment, he raised his eyes and saw Abraham a long way off, and Lazarus close beside him. So he shouted, ‘Father Abraham, show me mercy! Send Lazarus here. Let him wet the end of his finger with water and cool my tongue, for this flame is causing me terrible pain.’ But Abraham answered, ‘My child, remember: while you were alive you had your good things, and Lazarus in the same way had the bad things. Now here he finds comfort, and you are suffering. What is more, a vast gulf lies fixed between us and you. Anyone who wanted to go across from here to you could not, and no one can cross from your side to ours.’ ‘Then, father, I ask you this,’ he said. ‘Send him to my father’s house, where I have five brothers. He can give them a solemn warning, so that they do not come to this place of torment as well.’ But Abraham said, ‘Moses and the prophets are there for them. Let your brothers listen to what they say.’ He answered, ‘That is not enough, father Abraham. But if someone goes to them from among the dead, they will repent.’ Abraham said to him, ‘If they will not listen to Moses and the prophets, then even someone rising from the dead will not persuade them.’”

fields.title: Luke 17
fields.body_html:
Stumbling, forgiveness and faith

Jesus said to his disciples, “Things that trip people up and lead them into sin will certainly come. But how terrible for the one who brings them! It would be better for that person to be thrown into the sea with a millstone tied around their neck than to make one of these little ones stumble. Be on your guard. When your brother or sister does wrong, warn them. Then if they repent, forgive them. Seven times in one day they may wrong you, and seven times come back and say, ‘I repent.’ Even so, forgive them.”

The apostles said to the Lord, “Give us more faith!” The Lord answered, “If you had faith the size of a mustard seed, you could tell this mulberry tree, ‘Tear yourself up by the roots and be planted in the sea,’ and it would do as you say.

Servants who only did their duty

Imagine that one of you has a servant who has been out plowing or tending the sheep. When he comes in from the field, will you tell him, ‘Come straight in and take your place at the table’? Will you not tell him instead, ‘Make me something to eat. Then tie on your apron and serve me while I have my meal. You can eat and drink afterward’? The master does not owe the servant any thanks for doing what he was ordered to do, does he? It is the same with you. When you have done everything you were ordered to do, say, ‘We are unworthy servants. We have done no more than we were bound to do.’”

Ten healed, one returns

As Jesus made his way toward Jerusalem, he went through the region between Samaria and Galilee. As he came into a village, ten men with leprosy came toward him. They kept their distance and called out loudly, “Jesus! Master! Have mercy on us!” Jesus saw them and told them, “Go and let the priests examine you.” On their way there, they were made clean. One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, giving glory to God with a loud voice. He fell face down at the feet of Jesus, thanking him. And the man was a Samaritan. Jesus responded, “Ten men were made clean, were they not? So where are the other nine? Is this outsider the only one who came back to give glory to God?” Then he told him, “Stand up and go on your way. Your faith has made you well.”

Where the kingdom of God is

Once the Pharisees asked Jesus when the kingdom of God would come. He answered them, “The kingdom of God does not come in a way you can watch for and track. People will not say, ‘It is here!’ or ‘It is over there!’ For the kingdom of God is among you.”

The day the Son of Man is revealed

Then he said to the disciples, “There will be days when you ache to see even one day of the Son of Man, but you will not get to see it. People will tell you, ‘Look over there!’ or ‘Look here!’ Do not go out, and do not run after them. When lightning flashes, it lights up the sky from one edge to the other. That is how the Son of Man will be on his day. But before that, he must go through great suffering and be turned away by the people of this generation. What happened in Noah’s time will happen again in the days of the Son of Man. People were eating and drinking, taking wives and being given as wives, right up to the day Noah went into the ark. Then the flood came and wiped them all out. It was the same in Lot’s time. People ate and drank, bought and sold, planted and built. Then came the day Lot walked out of Sodom. Fire and sulfur fell like rain from heaven, and every one of them was destroyed. That is how it will be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. On that day anyone up on the roof must not go down into the house to get their things. In the same way, anyone out in the field must not turn around to fetch what is behind. Remember Lot’s wife. Anyone who tries to hold on to their life will lose it, and anyone who loses it will keep it alive. I tell you, that night two people will be sleeping in one bed. One will be taken, and the other will be left behind. Two women will be grinding grain together. One will be taken, and the other will be left behind.” They asked him, “Where will this happen, Lord?” He said to them, “Where the corpse lies, there the vultures will flock together.”

fields.title: Luke 18
fields.body_html:
A widow who kept coming

Jesus told them a parable about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart. He said, “There was once a judge in a certain city who did not fear God and had no regard for anyone. In that city there was also a widow who came to him again and again. She said, ‘Give me my rights against my opponent.’ For a while he refused. But later he said to himself, ‘I do not fear God and I have no regard for anyone. Still, this widow is such a nuisance that I will give her justice. If I do not, she will keep coming until she wears me out.’” The Lord said, “Listen to what the unjust judge says. Then surely God will give justice to the people he has chosen, when they call out to him day and night. Will he be slow to help them? I tell you, he will see them vindicated, and without delay. Even so, when the Son of Man comes, will he find this kind of faith on the earth?” There were some who relied on themselves, sure that they were righteous, and who looked down on all others. Jesus told them this parable. “Two men went up to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector. The Pharisee stood and prayed this prayer about himself: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity, who are swindlers, crooks and adulterers, or even like this tax collector. Twice every week I fast, and I give a tenth of everything I take in.’ The tax collector, though, kept back at a distance and would not even lift his eyes toward heaven. Instead he struck his chest again and again and said, ‘God, be merciful to me, the sinner!’ I tell you, it was this man, not the other, who went home put right with God. For everyone who lifts themselves up will be brought low, and the one who takes the low place will be lifted up.”

Children and the kingdom

People were even bringing their babies to him, so that he would touch them. The disciples saw it and began to scold them. But Jesus called them over and said, “Let the little children come to me, and do not try to stop them. The kingdom of God belongs to those who are like them. Truly I tell you, anyone who does not welcome the kingdom of God the way a child does will never get into it.”

A rich leader’s question

One of the leaders asked him, “Good Teacher, what do I have to do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus answered, “Why are you calling me good? No one is good but God alone. You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery. Do not murder. Do not steal. Do not give false testimony. Honor your father and your mother.’” The man replied, “I have kept every one of these from my youth.” Hearing this, Jesus told him, “You are still missing one thing. Sell all your possessions and hand out the money to the poor. Then you will have treasure in heaven. After that, come and follow me.” At these words the man was filled with sorrow, for he was a man of great wealth.

Seeing this, Jesus said, “What a hard thing it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! In fact, a camel could get through the eye of a needle more easily than a rich person could get into the kingdom of God.”

Those listening asked, “Then who can be saved?” He answered, “What human beings cannot do is possible for God.”

Peter said, “But we have given up what was ours and followed you!” He answered them, “Truly I tell you, anyone who has left a house, a wife, brothers, parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God is sure to be given back far more in this life, and in the age that is coming, eternal life.”

Going up to Jerusalem

Taking the Twelve aside, he told them, “We are now going up to Jerusalem, and all that the prophets wrote about the Son of Man will come to pass. He will be given over to the Gentiles, who will make fun of him, treat him shamefully and spit on him. After whipping him they will put him to death, and on the third day he will rise.” But the Twelve understood none of this. What he said was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what he meant.

A blind man at Jericho sees

Jesus was approaching Jericho. A blind man was sitting there beside the road, begging. He heard a crowd passing by and asked what it was all about. They told him, “Jesus of Nazareth is going by.” So he shouted, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” The people at the front of the crowd told him sternly to be quiet, but he cried out all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” Jesus stood still and gave orders for them to bring the man to him. When the man came near, Jesus asked him, “What would you like me to do for you?” He answered, “Lord, I want to see again.” Jesus told him, “See again. Your faith has made you well.” At once he could see, and he followed him, giving glory to God. All the people saw what happened, and they gave praise to God.

fields.title: Luke 19
fields.body_html:
Zacchaeus climbs a tree

Jesus entered Jericho and was making his way through the town. A man named Zacchaeus lived there. He was a chief tax collector, and he was rich. He was trying to see who Jesus was, but he could not see over the crowd, because he was a short man. So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore-fig tree to see him, since Jesus was going to come along that road. When Jesus reached the spot, he looked up and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry down. Today is the day I have to stay in your home.” So he hurried down and gladly welcomed him. Everyone who saw it began to mutter and complain. “He has gone to be a guest at the house of a sinner!” they said. But Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord, “Lord, see: half of what I own I am giving to the poor. And if I have taken anything from anyone by cheating, I am paying it back four times over.” Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this household. This man too is one of Abraham’s sons. The Son of Man came to look for what was lost and to save it.”

Ten servants and ten minas

As they listened to this, Jesus went on to tell them a parable. He did this because he was near Jerusalem, and they supposed that the kingdom of God was about to appear at once. So he said, “A man from a noble family traveled to a faraway country to be made king there, and then to come back home. Before he left, he called ten of his servants and gave them ten minas, one to each. ‘Put this money to work until I come back,’ he told them. But the people of his country hated him. They sent a delegation after him to say, ‘We do not want this man to be our king.’ He was made king and came back home. Then he sent for the servants to whom he had given the money, to find out what profit each had made by his trading. The first came and said, ‘Master, your mina has made ten minas more.’ ‘Excellent, good servant!’ he replied. ‘You have been trustworthy in a very small matter, so you will have authority over ten cities.’ The second came and said, ‘Master, your mina has earned five minas.’ To him too he said, ‘You will be over five cities.’ Then another came and said, ‘Master, here is your mina. I kept it put away in a piece of cloth. I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take out what you never put in, and you harvest what you never planted.’ He answered, ‘Your own words condemn you, you wicked servant! So you knew that I am a severe man, taking out what I never put in and harvesting what I never planted? Then why did you not put my money in the bank? Then when I came back, I would have collected it with interest.’ Then he said to those standing there, ‘Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has ten.’ ‘Master,’ they said, ‘he has ten minas already!’ ‘I tell you, everyone who has will be given more. But the one who has nothing will lose even what they have. As for these enemies of mine who did not want me as their king, bring them here and execute them in my presence.’”

The king comes riding on a colt

After saying this, Jesus went on ahead of them, going up to Jerusalem.

As he came near Bethphage and Bethany, by the hill called the Mount of Olives, he sent off two of the disciples. “Go to the village ahead of you,” he told them. “As you go into it, you will find a young donkey tied there, one that nobody has ever ridden. Untie it and bring it here. If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ tell them, ‘The Lord needs it.’” Those who had been sent went off and found things just as he had told them. As they were untying the young donkey, its owners asked them, “Why are you untying the donkey?” They answered, “The Lord needs it.” They brought the donkey to Jesus, threw their cloaks over it, and helped Jesus get on. As he rode along, people spread their cloaks on the road. As he came close to the city, where the road goes down the Mount of Olives, the whole crowd of his disciples began to praise God joyfully and loudly for all the mighty deeds they had seen. They shouted, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!” Some Pharisees in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell your disciples to stop!” He answered, “I tell you, if these people were silent, the very stones would shout.”

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem

When he came nearer and saw the city, he wept over it. “If only you too had known on this day the things that lead to peace!” he said. “But now they are hidden from your sight. For a time is coming for you when your enemies will build a siege wall against you. They will encircle you and press in on you from all sides. They will level you to the ground, you and your children inside you. They will leave no stone on top of another within you, because you did not recognize the time when God came to visit you.”

A house of prayer

Then Jesus went into the temple and began to throw out the people who were selling there. He said to them, “Scripture says, ‘My house will be a house of prayer.’ But you have turned it into a hideout for robbers.”

Every day he taught in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes wanted to kill him, and so did the leaders of the people. But they could find no way to do it, because all the people clung to him, listening to every word.

fields.title: Luke 20
fields.body_html:
A question about authority

One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and telling them the good news, the chief priests and the scribes came up to him, together with the elders. “Tell us,” they said to him, “what authority do you have to do these things? Who is it that gave you this authority?” He answered them, “I too will ask you a question. Tell me this: John’s baptism: did it come from heaven, or from people?” They discussed it among themselves and said, “If we answer, ‘From heaven,’ he will ask, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’ But if we answer, ‘From people,’ the whole crowd will stone us, because they are sure John was a prophet.” So they answered that they did not know where it came from. Jesus said to them, “Then I am not going to tell you either by what authority I do these things.”

The tenant farmers and the owner’s son

Then he told the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants. Then he went abroad and stayed away a long while. When harvest time came, he sent a servant to the tenants to collect his share of the vineyard’s crop. But the tenants beat him and sent him back with nothing. So he sent a second servant, but they beat this one as well, insulted him, and sent him off with nothing. Then he sent a third, and they wounded this one and threw him out. Then the master of the vineyard said, ‘What am I to do? I will send my son, the one I love. It may be that they will show him respect.’ But the tenants saw him coming and talked it over among themselves. ‘This is the one who will inherit,’ they said to each other. ‘If we kill him, the property will be ours.’ So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. So what will the master of the vineyard do to them? He will come and put these tenants to death, and give the vineyard to others.” Hearing this, the people cried out, “May that never happen!” Jesus looked straight at them and said, “Then what is the meaning of the words that are written, ‘The stone the builders discarded has become the main stone at the corner’? All who fall on that stone will be smashed, and if it falls on someone, it will grind that person to dust.” The scribes and the chief priests wanted to get their hands on him then and there, but they were afraid of the people. They understood that he had aimed this parable at them.

Paying tribute to Caesar

They watched him closely and sent agents who played the part of honest, devout men. Their aim was to seize on some word of his and use it to deliver him into the governor’s power and jurisdiction. So they put a question to him: “Teacher, we are sure that you are correct in what you say and teach. No one’s rank sways you, and you teach the way of God with truth. Does the law allow us to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?” But he saw through their trickery and said to them, “Let me see a denarius. Whose likeness and whose inscription does it carry?” They answered, “Caesar’s.” He said to them, “Then pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God.” So with the people looking on, they found nothing in his words to seize on. His answer left them amazed, and they had nothing more to say.

A question about the resurrection

Then some Sadducees came up, men who say there is no resurrection, and put a question to him: “Teacher, Moses gave us this law in writing: when someone’s brother dies married but without children, the surviving brother is to marry the widow and raise children for the one who died. There were once seven brothers. The first married and died without having a child. Then the second and the third married her, and so on with all seven: each one died and left no children. Last of all, the woman died too. So when the dead rise, whose wife will she be? All seven of them had her as a wife.”

Jesus answered them, “In this age, men take wives and women are given to husbands. But those who are judged worthy to have a share in the age to come and in the rising from the dead neither take wives nor are given to husbands. They will never die again, for they are equal to the angels; and having had their share in the resurrection, they are children of God. And that the dead are raised, even Moses made plain in the account of the burning bush, where he calls the Lord ‘the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.’ God is not a God of dead people but of living people, since all of them live in relation to him.” Some of the scribes responded, “Teacher, that was a fine answer.” From then on they did not dare put any more questions to him.

David’s son and David’s Lord

Then he said to them, “How can people say that Christ is the son of David? David himself says in the book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord: “Take your seat at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet as a footstool.”‘ So if David calls him ‘Lord,’ how can he be David’s son?” In the hearing of all the people, he said to the disciples, “Be on your guard against the scribes. They like to parade in long robes. They love it when people greet them in the marketplaces, and they love the front seats in the synagogues and the best couches at dinners. They swallow up the property of widows, and they pray at great length to cover it up. These men will receive the heavier judgment.”

fields.title: Luke 21
fields.body_html:
A poor widow’s gift

Jesus looked up and watched as rich people dropped their gifts into the temple’s offering chests. He also noticed a needy widow drop in two pennies. Then he said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has given more than all the rest. Every one of them gave out of their surplus. But she, out of her need, has given the whole of what she had to live on.”

Not one stone on another

Some people were talking about the temple: how fine its stones were, and how it was decorated with gifts given to God. Jesus said, “You are looking at all this. But days are coming when it will all be torn down, and not a stone will stay standing on another.”

They put a question to him: “Teacher, when will these things be? And what sign will there be when they are about to take place?” He answered, “Take care that no one leads you astray. Many will come claiming my name and saying, ‘I am the one!’ and, ‘The time has come near!’ Do not go after them. When you hear about wars and rebellions, do not panic. All this has to happen first, but it does not mean that the end comes at once.” Then he went on to tell them, “One nation will go to war with another, and one kingdom with another. There will be powerful earthquakes, and in place after place famines and diseases. Fearful things will happen, and great signs will appear in the sky.

Before all that, however, they will arrest you and hunt you down. They will hand you over to synagogues and to prisons, and you will be led off to stand before kings and governors for the sake of my name. This will give you the chance to bear witness. So settle it in your hearts: do not plan your defense in advance. I myself will give you the words and the wisdom to speak, and not one of your opponents will be able to stand against them or argue back. You will be handed over even by your own parents and brothers and sisters, your relatives and your friends, and some of you they will kill. You will be hated by everyone on account of my name. Yet not a single hair of your head will be lost. Hold out to the end, and so win your lives.

Jerusalem surrounded

When you see Jerusalem with armies encamped all around it, then be sure that it will soon be laid waste. Then people in Judea should run for the hills. Those inside the city should leave it, and those out in the fields should not go back in. For these are the days of punishment, when everything that is written will come true. How terrible it will be in those days for women who are pregnant or nursing a baby! Great hardship will come on the land, and wrath on this people. They will be cut down by the sword and carried off as captives to every nation. Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles have run their course.

The Son of Man comes in a cloud

Signs will appear in the sun, the moon and the stars. On the earth whole nations will be gripped with distress, not knowing where to turn as the sea roars and heaves. Fear will drain the strength out of people as they wait for what is coming on the world, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken. And then people will see the Son of Man come in a cloud with power and with great glory. As soon as these things start to happen, straighten up and look up, for the day of your redemption is almost here.”

Learn from the fig tree

He told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree, and at all the trees. Once they burst into leaf, you only need to look at them to know that summer is near. It is the same with you. When you see these things happening, be sure of this: the kingdom of God is near. Truly I tell you, all of this will happen before this generation is gone. Heaven and earth will disappear, but my words will last forever.

Stay awake and pray

Be on your guard. Do not let your hearts grow dull with wild parties and drinking and the worries of everyday life, or that day will catch you off guard, like a trap that snaps shut. It will come on everyone who lives anywhere on earth. Keep watch at all times, and pray for strength to come safely through all that is going to happen, and to stand before the Son of Man.”

By day Jesus was teaching in the temple. At night he would go out of the city and spend the night on the hill known as the Mount of Olives. At dawn all the people would come to him in the temple to listen.

fields.title: Luke 22
fields.body_html:
The leaders plot, and Judas joins them

Now the time was drawing near for the feast of Unleavened Bread, which is known as the Passover. The chief priests and the scribes were looking for some way to put him to death, because they were afraid of the people.

Then Satan entered into Judas, the one called Iscariot, who was one of the Twelve. He went off and talked with the chief priests and the temple officers about how he could betray him to them. They were glad and agreed to pay him money. He accepted, and from then on he looked for a good chance to betray him to them when no crowd was around.

Preparing the Passover

Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, the day when the Passover lamb had to be killed as a sacrifice. So Jesus sent Peter and John with these instructions: “Go and get the Passover meal ready for us to eat.” They asked him, “Where do you want us to get it ready?” He told them, “As you go into the city, you will be met by a man who is carrying a jar of water. Follow him into whatever house he goes into. Say to the owner of the house, ‘The Teacher asks you, “Which is the guest room where I can eat the Passover with my disciples?”‘ He will show you a large room upstairs, with everything laid out. Get the meal ready there.” So they went off and found it all just as he had said, and they got the Passover ready.

The Passover meal with the apostles

When the hour came, he took his place at the table, and the apostles with him. And he said to them, “How I have longed to eat this Passover with you before I suffer! For I tell you, I will not eat it again until it finds its fulfillment in the kingdom of God.” Then he took a cup, gave thanks, and said, “Take this and share it among yourselves. I tell you, from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.” Then he took bread, and after giving thanks he broke it and handed it to them, saying, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” In the same way he took the cup after the meal, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, poured out for you. Yet the hand of the man who is betraying me is here with me on the table. The Son of Man is going the way that has been marked out for him. But how terrible it will be for that man who betrays him!” They began to ask one another which of them it could possibly be who was going to do such a thing.

The greatest is the one who serves

A quarrel also broke out among them over which of them was to be thought the greatest. But he said to them, “The kings of the Gentiles act as lords over their people, and those who hold power over them are given the title ‘Benefactor’. With you it must not be this way. Instead, the greatest among you must become like the youngest, and the one in charge like the one who waits on others. Think about it: who is greater, the guest who lies at the table, or the one who serves the meal? Surely the one at the table. Yet here I am among you as the one who serves.

You are the ones who have stood by me through my trials. And just as my Father has granted me a kingdom, so I grant one to you. You will eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and you will sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. Simon, Simon, Satan has demanded to have all of you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, so that your faith will not give out. And you, once you have turned back, must strengthen your brothers.” Peter answered him, “Lord, I am ready to go to prison with you, and even to die with you.” Jesus replied, “I tell you, Peter, before a rooster crows today, you will have said three times that you do not know me.”

Purse, bag and sword

Then he said to them, “When I sent you out with no money bag, no traveler’s bag and no sandals, were you short of anything?” They said, “Not a thing.” He said to them, “But now, whoever has a money bag must take it along, and a traveler’s bag too. And whoever has no sword should sell their cloak and buy one. For I tell you, what is written must be fulfilled in me: ‘He was counted among the lawless.’ Yes, what was written about me is reaching its end.” They said, “Lord, look, here are two swords.” And he said to them, “That is enough.”

Not my will but yours

Then he left and went, as was his habit, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples went with him. When he arrived at the place, he said to them, “Pray that you do not come into temptation.” Then he went off from them about a stone’s throw, knelt down, and began to pray, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Yet let your will be done, not mine.” Then an angel from heaven appeared to him and gave him strength. In his anguish he prayed all the more intensely, and his sweat became like thick drops of blood dripping down onto the ground. When he got up from prayer and came back to the disciples, he found them asleep, worn down by their grief. And he said to them, “Why are you sleeping? Get up and pray, so that you will not come into temptation.”

Judas comes with a crowd

While he was still speaking, a crowd appeared. The man called Judas, one of the Twelve, was leading them, and he came up to Jesus to kiss him. But Jesus said to him, “Judas, is it with a kiss that you betray the Son of Man?” When those around him saw what was going to happen, they said, “Lord, should we strike with our swords?” And one of them struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear. But Jesus said, “Enough of this!” And he touched the man’s ear and healed him. Then Jesus said to the chief priests, the officers of the temple guard and the elders who had come out against him, “Did you have to come out with swords and clubs, as if I were a bandit? Day after day I was with you in the temple, and you did not lift a hand against me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.”

Peter’s three denials

They seized him, led him away and brought him into the high priest’s house. Peter followed at a distance. People had lit a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down around it, and Peter sat among them. A servant girl saw him sitting in the firelight. She stared at him and said, “This man was with him too.” But he denied it. “Woman, I do not know him,” he said. A little later someone else saw him and said, “You are one of them too.” But Peter said, “Friend, I am not.” About an hour later another man insisted, “This is the truth: this fellow was with him. He is a Galilean too.” But Peter said, “Friend, I have no idea what you are talking about.” At that very moment, while he was still speaking, a rooster crowed. And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the Lord’s words, how he had told him, “Today, before a rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” He went outside and wept bitterly.

Blindfolded and mocked

The men who were guarding Jesus made fun of him as they beat him. They covered his eyes and kept asking him, “Prophesy! Who was it that struck you?” And they said many other insulting things against him.

Questioned by the council

At daybreak the elders of the people met together, both chief priests and scribes, and they took him away to their council. They said, “If you are the Christ, tell us.” But he said to them, “If I tell you, you will not believe. And if I ask you a question, you will not answer. But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” They all said, “So you are the Son of God?” He answered them, “You say that I am.” Then they said, “Why do we need any more witnesses? We have heard it ourselves from his own mouth.”

fields.title: Luke 23
fields.body_html:
Jesus is brought to Pilate

Then the whole assembly got up and brought him before Pilate. They started to bring charges against him: “We have found this man leading our nation astray. He forbids paying taxes to Caesar, and he claims to be Christ, a king.” So Pilate asked him, “Are you the king of the Jews?” He answered him, “You say so.” Pilate told the chief priests and the crowds, “I find this man guilty of nothing.” But they pressed the charge harder: “He is stirring up the people with his teaching all over Judea. He started in Galilee and has come all the way here.” When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was from Galilee. When he learned that he came under Herod’s authority, he sent him on to Herod, who was also in Jerusalem at that time. Herod was delighted when he saw Jesus. He had wanted to see him for a long time because of what he had heard about him, and he hoped to watch him perform some sign. He put question after question to him, but Jesus gave him no answer at all. The chief priests and the scribes stood by, accusing him fiercely. Herod and his soldiers treated him with scorn and made fun of him. Herod had him dressed in a bright robe and sent him back to Pilate. That same day Herod and Pilate became friends. Until then there had been hostility between them. Pilate called together the chief priests, the rulers and the people and said to them, “You brought this man before me on the charge that he was turning the people from their loyalty. I have questioned him in your presence, and I have found him guilty of none of the things you accuse him of. Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Plainly he has done nothing that deserves death. So I will have him flogged and then let him go.”

The crowd asks for Barabbas

But the whole crowd shouted as one, “Take this man away! Set Barabbas free for us!” He had been put in prison for a riot that broke out in the city, and for murder. Pilate spoke to them once more, because he wanted to set Jesus free. But they kept shouting back, “Crucify him! Crucify him!” For the third time he said to them, “Why? What wrong has this man done? I have found no reason to put him to death. So I will have him flogged and then let him go.” But they pressed their demand with loud shouts, calling for him to be crucified, and their shouting won the day. So Pilate ruled that what they asked for should be done. He set free the man they asked for, the one who had been put in prison for revolt and murder. But Jesus he gave up to them to do as they wished.

On the way to the Skull

As they led him away, they took hold of a man named Simon from Cyrene, who was coming in from the countryside. They laid the cross on him and made him carry it behind Jesus.

A large crowd of the people followed him, among them women who were mourning and wailing for him. Jesus turned toward them and said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, it is not me you should be weeping over. Weep over yourselves and over your children. Days are coming when people will say, ‘Blessed are the women who could not have children, the wombs that never gave birth and the breasts that never fed a baby.’ Then they will start saying to the mountains, ‘Fall on us!’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us!’ For if this is how they treat wood that is green, what will become of wood that is dry?” Two other men, both criminals, were also led out with him to be executed. When they reached the place called the Skull, they crucified him there, with the criminals, one at his right hand and one at his left. Jesus kept saying, “Father, forgive them. They do not know what they are doing.” They shared out his clothes among themselves by casting lots. The people stood there looking on. The rulers joined in the scoffing. “He saved others,” they said. “So let him save himself, if this man is God’s Christ, the one God chose.” The soldiers made fun of him as well. They came up and held out sour wine to him, saying, “If you are the king of the Jews, save yourself!” Above him there was also a written notice: “This is the king of the Jews.”

The two criminals

One of the criminals hanging beside him kept abusing him. “You are the Christ, are you not? Then save yourself, and us too!” But the other criminal rebuked him: “Have you no fear even of God, when you are under the same sentence of death? For us it is fair: we are paying the due price for what we did. But this man has done nothing amiss.” Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come in your kingdom.” Jesus answered him, “Truly I tell you, this very day you will be with me in paradise.”

Darkness at midday and Jesus’ last words

It was already about midday when darkness covered the whole land, and it lasted until three in the afternoon. The light of the sun failed, and the curtain in the sanctuary was torn down the middle. Then Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Father, I place my spirit in your hands.” With these words he breathed out his last breath.

The centurion saw what had taken place, and he gave glory to God, saying, “Truly this man was righteous.” All the crowds who had gathered to watch this spectacle saw what had happened, and they turned back home, striking their breasts. Everyone who knew him stood far off. The women who had come with him from Galilee were standing there too, and they saw these things.

Joseph lays Jesus in a tomb

There was a man named Joseph who was a member of the council, a good and righteous man who had not given his consent to what the council planned and did. He came from Arimathea, a town of the Jews, and he was waiting for the kingdom of God. He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. He took the body down from the cross and wrapped it in a linen sheet. Then he laid him in a tomb cut out of the rock, where no one had ever been buried. It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was drawing near. The women who had come with him from Galilee went after Joseph. They saw the tomb and the way his body was laid there. Then they went back and got spices and fragrant oils ready.

On the Sabbath they rested, as the commandment required.

fields.title: Luke 24
fields.body_html:
Very early on the first day of the week, at the first light of dawn, the women came to the tomb. They brought with them the spices they had made ready. They found that the stone had been rolled back from the tomb. But when they went inside, they found no body there. They were at a loss to know what this meant. Then two men were standing by them, their clothing flashing with light. The women were terrified and kept their faces bowed to the ground. But the men said to them, “Why are you looking among the dead for the one who is alive? He is not here; he has been raised. Remember what he told you when he was still in Galilee. He said that the Son of Man had to be handed over to sinful people and be crucified, and on the third day rise again.” Then his words came back to them. They went back from the tomb and reported all of this to the Eleven and to everyone else. The women were Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the others who were with them. They kept telling the apostles about these things. But to the apostles the report sounded like nonsense, and they would not believe the women.

Peter, though, got up and ran to the tomb. He bent down to look in and saw nothing but the linen wrappings. Then he went home, amazed at what had taken place.

Two disciples walk to Emmaus

On that very day two of them were walking to Emmaus, a village about seven miles from Jerusalem. They were deep in conversation about all that had happened. While they were talking it over and debating, Jesus himself came near and began to walk with them. But their eyes were held back, and they did not know him. He said to them, “What is this conversation you are having with each other as you walk?” They stopped walking, and their faces were gloomy. One of them, a man named Cleopas, answered him, “Can you be the one visitor in Jerusalem who has not heard what has gone on there in the past few days?” “What things?” he asked them. They said to him, “About Jesus from Nazareth. He was a prophet, a man whose deeds and words had great power in the eyes of God and of all the people. And our chief priests and leaders handed him over to be condemned to death, and they crucified him. Our hope was that he was the one who would redeem Israel. And on top of all that, this is now the third day since it happened. And then some women of our company gave us a shock. They went to the tomb at first light and found that his body was gone. They came back and said they had even seen angels in a vision, angels who say that he is alive. Some of our people went to the tomb as well. They found everything the way the women had described it, but they saw nothing of him.” Then he said to them, “You are without understanding, and your hearts are slow to believe all that the prophets said! Christ had to suffer these things and enter into his glory, did he not?” Then, starting with Moses and going on through all the prophets, he explained to them what was written about himself in every part of the Scriptures.

They came near the village they were heading for, and he gave the impression of going on farther. But they would not let him go on. “Stay with us,” they said. “Evening is coming, and the daylight is already fading.” He went inside to stay with them. When he had taken his place at the table with them, he took the bread and said the blessing. Then he broke it and handed it to them. Then their eyes were opened and they knew who he was. And he could no longer be seen. They said to each other, “Did we not feel our hearts on fire inside us while he talked with us on the road and laid the Scriptures open to us?” Without delay they got up and went back to Jerusalem. They found the Eleven gathered with their companions, who were saying, “The Lord has truly been raised, and he has appeared to Simon!” The two then told their own story: what took place on the road, and how he became known to them in the breaking of the bread.

Flesh and bones

As they were talking about all this, Jesus himself was standing among them. But they were alarmed and filled with fear, for they thought they were looking at a spirit. He said to them, “Why are you so shaken? Why are these doubts coming up in your hearts? Look at my hands and my feet, and see that it is really I. Feel me and see. Spirits have no flesh and bones; you can see that I do.” After saying this, he let them see his hands and feet. Their joy and amazement were so great that they still could not believe it. Then he asked them, “Do you have something here to eat?” They handed him a piece of grilled fish. He took it and ate it while they watched.

Everything written about him

Then he said to them, “This is what I was telling you when I was still with you: whatever the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms have written about me must be fulfilled.” Then he opened their minds to make sense of the Scriptures. He told them, “This is what stands written: Christ is to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and in his name repentance and the forgiveness of sins are to be announced to all the nations, starting from Jerusalem. You are witnesses to these things. I am sending upon you what my Father promised. As for you, remain here in the city until power from on high clothes you.”

Blessing at Bethany

He led them out until they were near Bethany. There he raised his hands and blessed them. He was still blessing them when he parted from them and was borne up into heaven. They bowed down in worship before him, then made their way back to Jerusalem with great joy. And they spent all their time in the temple, blessing God.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
He led them out until they were near Bethany. There he raised his hands and blessed them. He was still blessing them when he parted from them and was borne up into heaven. They bowed down in worship before him, then made their way back to Jerusalem with great joy. And they spent all their time in the temple, blessing God.

— Luke 24:50–53

Luke’s Gospel ends where it began, in the temple, with people praising God. In the first chapter an old priest came out of the sanctuary unable to speak, and could not give the blessing the people were waiting for. In the last chapter Jesus lifts his hands and blesses his disciples, and they go back to the temple full of joy. The blessing Zechariah could not give has been given.

The question the book leaves with you

Luke is full of people who are found: shepherds, a widow, a sinful woman, a Samaritan leper, a chief tax collector up a tree, a criminal on a cross. And it is full of people who must decide whether to come in. The clearest of them is the elder brother in the parable of the lost son. His father comes out to plead with him, and says:

His father answered, ‘My child, you are with me always, and all that is mine belongs to you. But it was only right to celebrate and rejoice, for this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.’”

— Luke 15:31–32

Jesus does not tell us whether he went in. The story was told to people who grumbled that Jesus welcomed sinners, and it leaves them, and us, standing at the door of the feast. Luke’s Gospel is good news for the lost. But it asks those who think they were never lost whether they will rejoice when others are found.

The two on the road to Emmaus leave another question. They walked beside the risen Jesus for seven miles and did not know him. Their hearts burned as he opened the Scriptures, and their eyes were opened when he broke the bread. Luke wrote, perhaps, for readers who would never see Jesus as the apostles did. He tells them where he is to be found: in the Scriptures opened, at the table, among those who gather in his name.

Where the book points

It points, first, to Jerusalem and beyond. The risen Jesus tells his disciples that repentance and the forgiveness of sins are to be announced in his name “to all the nations, starting from Jerusalem.” They are to wait in the city until power from on high clothes them. Luke’s Gospel is the first of two volumes, and the second, the Acts of the Apostles, begins with that promise kept and follows the message from Jerusalem to Rome.

It points, second, to a way of life. The Jesus of Luke’s Gospel eats with outcasts, notices widows, warns the rich and prays all night. He tells his followers to pick up their cross “every day”, to show compassion as their Father shows compassion, and to go and do as the Samaritan did. To read Luke and not be changed in how we treat the poor and the outsider is not really to have read it.

And it points to joy. The book that begins with an angel announcing “a great joy that is for all the people” ends with disciples going home “with great joy”. Between them stand a shepherd carrying a lost sheep home on his shoulders, a woman calling her neighbours to celebrate a coin, and a father running down the road.

Where to go from here

Luke’s stories have been preached more than almost any others in the Bible, and many of the best sermons on them are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On the birth of Jesus (chapter 2). Martin Luther’s The Story of the Birth of Jesus (2:1–14) and John Newton’s The Angel’s Message and Song (2:8–14).
  • On Martha and Mary (10:38–42). Augustine of Hippo’s sermon Martha and Mary.
  • On prayer. Andrew Murray’s With Christ in the School of Prayer, which begins with the disciples’ request, “Lord, teach us how to pray” (11:1), and J. C. Ryle’s Do You Pray? (18:1).
  • On the great invitation (chapter 14). Charles H. Spurgeon’s Compel Them to Come In (14:23).
  • On the lost son (chapter 15). Alexander Maclaren’s The Prodigal and His Father (15:11–24), and Frederick W. Robertson’s The Prodigal and His Brother (15:11–32), which gives the elder brother his due.
  • On money (chapter 16). John Wesley’s The Use of Money (16:9).
  • On the tears of Jesus (19:41–42). Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s The Saviour’s Tears over the Lost.
  • On the cross. D. L. Moody’s The Dying Thief (23:39–43).
  • On the risen Lord (chapter 24). Andrew Murray’s Jesus Himself, on the two disciples whose eyes were opened (24:31), and John Bunyan’s The Jerusalem Sinner Saved, on the command to preach “starting from Jerusalem” (24:47).

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Luke in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this Gospel.

But the best next step is the one Luke himself intended. Turn the page to his second book, the Acts of the Apostles, and watch what happened when the promise of the Father came. And then come back to the first, and read it again, listening for the word that runs all through it, today: the day of the Saviour’s birth, the day salvation came to Zacchaeus’s house, and the day Jesus promised to the man dying beside him. It is meant for you too:

Jesus answered him, “Truly I tell you, this very day you will be with me in paradise.”

— Luke 23:43
